18	# PropGen: Automated Property Generation for Property-Based Testing of Mobile Apps
19	
20	- Authors: Xiong, Yiheng; Song, Shiwen; Ma, Bo; Su, Ting; Xie, Xiaofei
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837536 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837536
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). The PDF is arXiv v2 (8 Oct 2026) carrying the ASE '26 camera-ready header and DOI (p. 1); peer-reviewed (received 2026-03-26, accepted 2026-06-18, p. 13).
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Automate the construction of properties for property-based testing (PBT) of mobile apps with LLMs. A *property* here is a rule of the form precondition -> interaction -> expected postcondition that must hold whenever it applies; PBT then generates many GUI event sequences and checks whether the rule is violated (p. 1, p. 3).
30	- [A] Motivation: non-crashing functional bugs lack explicit test oracles; PBT can expose them, but writing properties by hand is "difficult and expensive", and apps rarely have specifications (p. 1). Asking an LLM directly for properties is unreliable because, without evidence of how the app behaves, "LLMs tend to hallucinate properties that the app never satisfies" (p. 2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [V] RQ1: effectiveness in exploring app functionalities and generating valid properties; RQ2: how often properties are imprecise (cause false positives) and how well refinement fixes them; RQ3: whether generated properties find new functional bugs; RQ4: comparison with prior functional-testing techniques in finding new bugs (p. 6).
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] Tool design plus empirical evaluation on 12 Android apps, with human annotation of validity, comparison against baselines, and bug reporting to developers (p. 6-8).
37	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] PropGen has three stages (p. 3-6): (1) **hypothesis-guided exploration**: an MLLM looks at the screenshot (with numbered widgets from the accessibility tree), app name and activity names, and proposes candidate functionalities each tied to a triggering widget; PropGen executes them step by step, the MLLM labels each step success/fail/complete, and traces are summarised into "behavioral evidence" (state before, event, state after, state diff, outcome); random exploration is used when no unexplored hypothesis remains (p. 4-5); (2) **property synthesis**: the MLLM first writes a natural-language property (precondition P, interaction I, postcondition Q) from the evidence, then translates it into executable code for the PBT tool Kea (p. 6); (3) **feedback-driven refinement**: for properties whose reported violations are *manually confirmed* false positives, the LLM locates which of P, I or Q is imprecise using the source trace and the failing run, and edits only that part (p. 4, p. 6).
38	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] RQ1: DroidAgent (LLM-based functionality exploration) and a naive LLM baseline that writes 20 properties per app from the app's official description without running the app (p. 7). RQ4: Genie, Odin (automated differential oracles), PBFDroid (PBT for data-manipulation functionalities) and VisionDroid (LLM multi-agent functional bug detection) (p. 7).
39	
40	## 4. Dataset and sample
41	- Data source(s): [V] 12 popular open-source Android apps (e.g. OmniNotes, Markor, AnkiDroid, NewPipe), 57,529 to 403,785 LOC; GitHub stars 1.1K-37.5K (p. 7).
42	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 12 apps. Units of analysis: 1,282 functionalities inferred by PropGen (575 by DroidAgent), 985 generated properties, 240 naive-baseline properties, 127 imprecise properties, 25 new bugs (p. 8-10).
43	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Eight apps adopted from prior functional-bug studies, excluding apps no longer runnable/maintained or functionally similar to already chosen ones; four more popular open-source Google Play apps added "to further improve diversity" (p. 6-7). No power or sample-size reasoning reported.
44	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We have made all the artifacts publicly available" (p. 11), Zenodo artifact doi:10.5281/zenodo.21770804 (p. 13). Not checked by us.
45	
46	## 5. Experimental setup
47	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Ubuntu 22.04, 192 CPU cores (AMD EPYC 9654), official Android 11 Pixel emulators; GPT-5.2 (snapshot gpt-5.2-2025-12-11) as backend MLLM for PropGen and DroidAgent with default decoding (temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0); 3 h per app for evidence construction and property synthesis, then 6 h of Kea PBT per app (p. 7). Built on DroidBot, uiautomator2 and ADB; mainly Python and JavaScript (p. 6). RQ4 time budgets aligned: 9 h per app for Genie, Odin and VisionDroid; 6 h testing for PBFDroid after the authors manually wrote its DMF properties (p. 8). DroidAgent's time budget is not stated explicitly (not reported).
48	- Human annotation: [V] two graduate students in software engineering (each at least four years of Android experience), not co-authors, labelled independently; Cohen's kappa 0.91 (functionality validity), 0.82 (execution correctness), 0.81 (property validity); disagreements then resolved by discussion (p. 7).
49	- Code availability: [A] artifacts released on Zenodo (p. 11, p. 13).
50	
51	## 6. Evaluation metrics
52	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
53	  - [V] **Functionality validity**: share of inferred functionalities that really exist in the app (human judged from screenshot) (p. 7).
54	  - [V] **Execution correctness**: share of inferred functionalities whose executed event sequence actually realises them (human judged) (p. 7).
55	  - [V] **Property validity**: property is valid only if every referenced widget/event appears in its source trace (automated groundedness check) and annotators judge P, I and Q faithful to the intended functionality (p. 7). Chosen because "mobile apps lack ground-truth specifications" (p. 7). Validity does not imply precision (p. 7).
56	  - [V] **Refinement success**: revised property must (a) still hold on its source trace, (b) no longer raise the spurious violation, and (c) be confirmed valid and intent-preserving by humans (p. 8).
57	  - [V] **New bugs**: manually confirmed, previously unreported functional bugs, reported to developers (p. 8); for RQ4 also a manual **scope analysis** of whether each prior tool's oracle could in principle detect each bug, partly validated by consulting authors of Genie, Odin and PBFDroid (p. 8).
58	  - [V] **Cost**: tokens and USD per LLM call and per app (p. 9).
59	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; counts and percentages from a single run per tool and app (p. 8-10). Only inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) is reported (p. 7).
60	
61	## 7. Key findings
62	1. PropGen inferred 1,282 functionalities, 1,210 valid (94.4%) and 977 correctly executed (76.2%), vs DroidAgent 575 inferred, 491 valid (85.4%), 187 correctly executed (32.5%) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9).
63	2. PropGen generated 985 properties, 912 valid (92.6%; 78.7%-98.8% per app) — [V] (p. 8). The naive LLM baseline (app description only) produced 240 properties, none valid, because it referenced non-existent widgets — [V] (p. 9).
64	3. 127 properties caused false positives during PBT; 118 (92.9%) were successfully refined, mostly by changing the postcondition (64) or precondition (53), only 1 by changing the interaction; of 9 failures, 5 were misdiagnoses and 4 drifted from the original intent — [V] (p. 9).
65	4. Properties found 25 previously unknown functional bugs in the latest app versions; 5 fixed by developers at writing time; categories: functionality does not take effect (12), state inconsistency (6), unexpected wrong behaviour (4), navigation failure (3) — [V] (p. 9-10).
66	5. Of the 25 bugs, only 7 (28%) were in the detection scope of the four prior tools and 3 (12%) were rediscovered; the prior tools together found 13 unknown bugs, of which PropGen missed 10 — [V] (p. 10). [A] The approaches are "complementary rather than substitutable" (p. 10).
67	6. Cost: about $14.86 and 6,364k tokens per app for PropGen vs $13.01 and 5,109k tokens for DroidAgent; refinement about $0.02 per property — [V] (p. 9).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- [A] Manual inspection of functionalities and properties may introduce subjectivity and bias; mitigated by two independent annotators and consensus (p. 11).
71	- [A] The 12 apps may not represent the diversity of real-world apps; a larger and broader set is planned (p. 11).
72	- [A] Open-source apps may be in GPT-5.2's training data; mitigated by checking that none of the 25 bugs was previously reported, and by noting that six of the 12 tested builds were released after the model's training cutoff and still yielded bugs (p. 11).
73	- [A] Failure modes: the MLLM sometimes proposes non-existent functionalities, executions may not finish within the step budget or are labelled successful too early, and synthesis occasionally hallucinates widgets despite grounding (p. 9). PropGen generates only one property per functionality and lacks the differential oracles of Genie/Odin (p. 10).
74	- [A] A pre-existing app fault could in principle corrupt generated or refined properties; risk argued to be limited because properties come only from successful traces and refinements are human-confirmed (p. 10-11).
75	
76	## 9. Limitations we identified
77	- [I] **Not fully automatic.** Refinement is triggered only after a human confirms a violation is a false positive (p. 4, p. 6), and bug confirmation is manual (p. 8). The cost of this human effort is not reported.
78	- [I] **Single run with temperature 1.0.** Each tool runs once per app (p. 8) with stochastic decoding (p. 7); no variance or repeat runs are reported, so it is unknown how stable the counts are.
79	- [I] **Weak naive baseline.** The naive baseline sees only the app's description, never the GUI (p. 7). Its 0/240 result shows that runtime evidence is needed, but does not test simpler runtime-grounded alternatives.
80	- [I] **Possible author-tool bias.** Kea and PBFDroid come from overlapping author groups (refs [52], [71], p. 12-13), and the PBFDroid properties used in RQ4 were written by the authors (p. 8). The scope analysis is manual (p. 8). These choices could favour PropGen, though consulting the original tool authors partly mitigates this.
81	- [I] **Contamination check is partial.** "Not previously reported" bugs (p. 11) do not show that the model lacks prior knowledge of app behaviour; app functionality, not bugs, is what the model may have memorised.
82	- [I] **Validity is judged against human understanding, not a specification** (p. 7). This is reasonable but means "valid" depends on annotators' familiarisation of at least fifteen minutes per app (p. 7).
83	
84	## 10. Threats to validity
85	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Same MLLM backend for PropGen and DroidAgent (p. 7) is a fair control. Budget alignment across tools in RQ4 (p. 8) is reasonable, but tools differ in design scope, which the authors address with the scope analysis (p. 8). Possible training-data exposure of open-source apps (p. 11).
86	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 12 open-source Android apps on emulators (p. 7); unclear transfer to iOS, web, closed-source or login/network-heavy apps.
87	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] "Valid" properties are grounded and faithful but may still be imprecise (p. 7); bug counts depend on each tool's oracle type, which the authors acknowledge ("Raw bug counts alone are therefore not directly comparable", p. 8).
88	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No statistical tests; 12 apps; single run (p. 8). High kappa values (0.81-0.91, p. 7) support annotation reliability.
89	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Good: model snapshot, decoding parameters, budgets, hardware and artifacts are reported (p. 7, p. 13). Proprietary model dependence and temperature 1.0 limit exact replication.
90	
91	## 11. Future research directions
92	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 9-11): evaluate on a larger and broader set of apps (p. 11); interact-then-infer functionality inference, activity transition graphs for step planning, explicit completion checks, post-synthesis widget checks (p. 9); richer context and an intent-verification step for refinement (p. 9); more properties per functionality and combining PropGen with specialised oracles (p. 10).
93	- Suggested by us [I]: use properties mined from an original app as a behavioural oracle for an AI-reconstructed version of that app (differential fidelity testing), and measure how many original-app properties the rebuild satisfies.
94	
95	## 12. Relevance to our research
96	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (indirect); RQ1 only tangentially. Not RQ3.
97	- How it informs our work [I]: PropGen does not generate or reconstruct applications, so it gives no direct evidence on fidelity or code quality of AI-built apps. Its value is as a method: it recovers behavioural specifications from a running black-box app (no source, no spec), which is exactly the kind of oracle a reverse-engineering study needs to check functional fidelity (RQ2, RQ5). Its result that an LLM without runtime observation produces 0 valid properties (p. 9) supports grounding any reconstruction or test generation in observed behaviour. Its evaluation design (independent annotators with kappa, scope analysis for oracle-dependent tools) is a good template for RQ4. Relevance is therefore medium.
98

18	# IWR-Bench: Can LVLMs reconstruct interactive webpage from a user interaction video?
19	
20	- Authors: Chen, Yang; Liu, Minghao; Shen, Yufan; Li, Yunwen; Huang, Tianyuan; Fang, Xinyu
21	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2509.24709 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24709
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Version read: arXiv v3, 19 Nov 2025 (p. 1). **Preprint, not peer-reviewed.**
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Introduce and formalise Interactive Webpage Reconstruction (IWR): given a video of a user interacting with a webpage plus the page's static assets, a model must generate code that reproduces both the visual appearance and the interactive behaviour seen in the video (p. 4, p. 5).
30	- [A] Motivation: existing webpage-to-code benchmarks are static (screenshot-to-code, e.g. Design2Code, WebSight) or treat interactions as single-step, stateless events (Interaction2Code), and do not provide the static assets needed for a realistic rebuild (p. 2, p. 6).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [A] Central question: "Can LVLMs reconstruct the dynamic, interactive functionalities of a webpage from observing a user interaction video?" (p. 2).
34	- No formal hypotheses are stated; the study is a descriptive benchmark evaluation (p. 7-9).
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus a cross-sectional comparison of 28 large vision-language models (LVLMs) on the same tasks, scored automatically by an "agent-as-a-judge" that replays a ground-truth action sequence on the generated page (p. 4, p. 6-8).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Each model receives the interaction video (sampled at 1 fps, max 64 frames) and a composite image of all crawled static assets, and must output one self-contained `index.html` with all HTML, CSS and JS; backend logic must be mocked in JS; no external libraries or fonts (p. 8, p. 20). Asset filenames are anonymised (e.g. `asset_001.png`) so models must match assets visually rather than by name (p. 5).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] No method baseline; the comparison is across 28 models in three groups: 17 proprietary MLLMs, 9 open-source MLLMs, 2 open-source video-specialised models; three models are also run in "thinking" (reasoning-enhanced) and non-thinking variants (p. 8).
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): [V] Live real-world websites; 113 tasks from 100 websites; videos recorded by trained annotators while a browser extension logs action type and parameters; static assets collected with automated crawlers plus manual inspection (p. 1, p. 5).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 113 tasks/videos; 1,001 actions in total (mean 8.9 per video); 620 actions carry a visual checkpoint and 403 carry a logical assertion; mean video length 35.4 s (max 172.9 s); 19 unique resolutions; 10.62% mobile (p. 6). Interaction-logic mix: L1 static 7.96%, L2 simple state 47.79%, L3 complex workflow 33.63%, L4 algorithm/game 10.62% (p. 3).
44	- Sampling / selection method: [V] 200 candidate tasks proposed by web-development experts -> deduplication and diversity balancing across domain, visual complexity and interaction logic -> 161 -> cross-verification by a second annotator and an LLM check of assertions -> disputed, ambiguous or overly trivial tasks removed -> 113 (p. 5-6). Exact criteria for "trivial" or "disputed" are not reported.
45	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Benchmark and evaluation code "will be made publicly available" at https://github.com/SIGMME/IWR-Bench (p. 1). We did not check whether the release happened.
46	
47	## 5. Experimental setup
48	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Video sampled at 1 fps, capped at 64 frames (longer videos uniformly downsampled); video frames and asset image given as a sequential multi-image input; "All other inference parameters utilize the default settings recommended by the model providers" (p. 8). A standard system prompt is used for all models (p. 18, p. 20). Evaluation executor built on the `browser-use` library; Gemini-2.5-Pro is the MLLM judge for logical assertions and for the high-level visual score (p. 6-7). Actions target elements by natural-language description rather than coordinates (p. 17). Number of runs per model, temperature/seed and variance: not reported.
49	- Code availability: [A] Announced for release at the GitHub link above (p. 1); not verified by us.
50	
51	## 6. Evaluation metrics
52	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
53	  - [V] **IFS (Interactive Functionality Score)** = successful actions / total actions; an action succeeds only if it is operationally feasible (target element found) and all its logical assertions pass (p. 7). Chosen to measure functional correctness, because pixel-wise metrics "cannot appraise functionality" (p. 3).
54	  - [V] **VFS (Visual Fidelity Score)** = macro-average over reached checkpoints with a visual flag of 0.5 x low-level score (mean of OCR Levenshtein text similarity and DINO cosine similarity) + 0.5 x high-level MLLM score (p. 7). The MLLM rubric weights Layout 10, Elements 15, Content and Text 40, Style 15, Overall 20 points (p. 20).
55	  - [V] **Final Score** = 0.7 x IFS + 0.3 x VFS, macro-averaged across the benchmark (p. 7).
56	  - [V] Weights w = 0.5 and alpha = 0.7 were chosen by grid search to maximise Spearman's rho with human judgements of 60 instances (20 random tasks x 3 random models) rated by five PhD-level students; best rho = 0.57 for VFS and 0.65 for the Final Score (p. 17).
57	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None for model comparisons; results are single point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests (p. 8-9). Only Spearman correlations are reported, for metric calibration (p. 17).
58	
59	## 7. Key findings
60	1. Interactive reconstruction from video is far from solved: GPT-5 is best with Final 36.35, IFS 24.39, VFS 64.25; no model exceeds 25 IFS — [V] (p. 8, p. 9).
61	2. Functionality lags visual fidelity for every model: e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 VFS 61.34 vs IFS 22.29; GPT-4o (latest) VFS 57.55 vs IFS 17.55 — [V] (p. 8, p. 9).
62	3. Clear hierarchy: proprietary models lead (Final 16.50-36.35); best open-source Qwen3-VL (thinking) 31.15; video-specialised models are lowest (VideoLLaMA3-7B 13.67, InternVideo-2.5-Chat-8B 10.07) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). [A] Authors conclude general multimodal reasoning and code generation matter more than video-specialised architectures (p. 9).
63	4. Reasoning ("thinking") variants give small gains in Final and IFS: Claude-Sonnet-4 34.62 vs 34.00 (IFS 23.65 vs 22.29); Claude-Opus-4 34.13 vs 33.33; Gemini-2.5-Pro 30.36 vs 30.31 — [V] (p. 9). Note: Gemini-2.5-Pro (thinking) has a lower VFS than its non-thinking variant (50.67 vs 53.18) (p. 8), so the gain is not "consistent" on every metric.
64	5. Performance drops sharply from static to interactive tasks: GPT-5 Final 61.85 on L1 static content vs 35.43 (L2), 35.12 (L3), 25.26 (L4 algorithm/game) — [V] (p. 17). Data-dense layouts (V4) are hardest visually (GPT-5 26.05 vs 44.77 on V1) (p. 18). Life & Community is the weakest domain and Entertainment & Media the strongest (GPT-5 22.80 vs 47.24) (p. 19).
65	6. Judge reliability: three PhD students watched the agent run on 100 random generated pages; agent evaluation failed in only three cases (ambiguous element descriptors), which were then fixed — [V] (p. 9).
66	7. Case studies show distinct failure points, e.g. a model completing filter and sort but failing "add to cart"; a model failing to merge tiles in a 2048 rebuild; missing first-step elements blocking all later actions — [V] (p. 19-21).
67	
68	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
69	- [A] The paper has no dedicated limitations or threats-to-validity section. The only self-critical points are in passing: an alternative weighting scheme for the Final Score "proved ineffective for differentiating model performance" (p. 7), and agent-evaluation failures caused by ambiguous element descriptors had to be corrected (p. 9).
70	- [A] An LLM was used for grammar correction and language refinement of the paper (p. 21).
71	
72	## 9. Limitations we identified
73	- [I] **No code-quality or maintainability measurement.** The task forces a single self-contained HTML file with no libraries (p. 20), and only behaviour and appearance are scored. The benchmark therefore says nothing about code structure, readability or maintainability (our RQ3), and the single-file format is far from how real apps are built.
74	- [I] **Judge overlap.** Gemini-2.5-Pro is both the assertion/visual judge (p. 7) and one of the evaluated models (p. 8). Self-preference bias is not tested; its mid-table rank makes a large bias unlikely, but it is not ruled out.
75	- [I] **Moderate human alignment, tuned in-sample.** The weights were chosen to maximise rho on the same 60 instances used to report rho = 0.57 / 0.65 (p. 17); there is no held-out check. These are moderate correlations, so the Final Score is only partly aligned with human judgement.
76	- [I] **No variance reporting.** Single point estimates with default sampling settings (p. 8) and no repeated runs reported; several model gaps are tiny (e.g. 30.36 vs 30.31, p. 9) and could be noise.
77	- [I] **Unclear failure propagation.** It is not stated whether a failed early action stops the replay or whether later actions are still attempted (p. 7); Case 4 suggests failures cascade (p. 21). This affects how IFS should be read.
78	- [I] **Possible contamination.** Tasks come from popular live websites (e.g. an IMDb mock in Figure 2, p. 2); models may have seen similar code in training. Asset anonymisation (p. 5) reduces name cues but not memorised page structure. Not discussed by the authors.
79	- [I] **Small strata.** L1 (about 9 tasks) and L4 (about 12 tasks), derived by us from the percentages on p. 3, give unstable per-category scores.
80	
81	## 10. Threats to validity
82	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Task filtering removed "overly trivial" and "disputed" tasks without stated criteria (p. 6), which may shift difficulty. All models get identical inputs and prompt (p. 18), which supports a fair comparison. Video downsampling to at most 64 frames (p. 8) may remove interaction evidence from long videos (max 172.9 s, p. 6); this affects all models equally but penalises long tasks.
83	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Front-end only, one HTML file, mocked backend (p. 20); 113 tasks. Results do not transfer directly to multi-file apps, backends, or native desktop/mobile apps.
84	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] IFS measures replay of one ground-truth trajectory, not general behavioural equivalence; VFS mixes OCR, DINO and an MLLM rubric in which text content carries 40 of 100 points (p. 20). Both are proxies for "functional fidelity" and "visual fidelity". The fixed alpha = 0.7 encodes a value judgement (functionality matters more), supported only by rho = 0.65 (p. 17).
85	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs, tests or repeated runs (p. 8-9); conclusions about small differences (thinking vs non-thinking) are not statistically supported.
86	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Prompts are published in the appendix (p. 20-21) and data and code are promised (p. 1). Proprietary model versions, default sampling settings and a proprietary judge model (p. 7) limit exact reproduction.
87	
88	## 11. Future research directions
89	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 9): focus on "temporal reasoning, dynamic asset binding, and robust code synthesis"; structured code generation and state management as key directions (p. 9).
90	- Suggested by us [I]: (a) add code-quality/maintainability measures (static analysis, modularity) to IWR-style tasks so fidelity and code quality are measured together (our RQ5); (b) allow multi-file or framework-based outputs and agentic, iterative generation; (c) report repeated runs with variance and a held-out human-alignment set; (d) use a judge model that is not also evaluated.
91	
92	## 12. Relevance to our research
93	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (indirectly). Not RQ3.
94	- How it informs our work [I]: IWR-Bench is a direct example of AI "reverse engineering" an application from observable behaviour (a video) rather than from a written spec, so it fits RQ1. Its main result, that functional correctness lags visual fidelity by a wide margin, is central evidence for RQ2. Its metric design (action replay with an agent judge, visual composite, human-calibrated weights) and weaknesses (no variance, in-sample calibration, judge overlap) inform RQ4 and our own study design. It illustrates the gap behind RQ5: fidelity is measured, but code quality and maintainability are not. The same "looks right, behaves wrong" pattern is reported across five platforms by [@bai2026recreationworld], which strengthens the finding.
95	
96	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
97	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
98	|---|---|---|---|---|
99	| RQ1 | LVLMs can be asked to rebuild an interactive webpage from a user-interaction video plus crawled assets (one HTML file); 28 models were evaluated on 113 real-site tasks | 5, 8 | V | weak |
100	| RQ2 | Best model (GPT-5) scores Final 36.35 with IFS 24.39 vs VFS 64.25; IFS < 25 for all 28 models | 8, 9 | V | moderate |
101	| RQ2 | Functional fidelity falls from static to algorithmic tasks (GPT-5 Final 61.85 on L1 vs 25.26 on L4) | 17 | V | weak |
102	| RQ2 | Reasoning-enhanced variants add little (e.g. Final 34.62 vs 34.00; 30.36 vs 30.31) | 9 | V | weak |
103	| RQ4 | Functional fidelity measured by agent replay of a ground-truth action sequence plus MLLM-judged assertions; visual fidelity by OCR + DINO + MLLM rubric | 7, 20 | V | weak |
104	| RQ4 | Metric weights tuned on 60 human-rated instances (5 raters); Spearman rho 0.57 (VFS) and 0.65 (Final), no held-out check | 17 | V | weak |
105	| RQ4 | Agent-judge errors in 3 of 100 manually observed runs | 9 | V | weak |
106	| RQ4 | No repeated runs, confidence intervals or significance tests for model comparisons | 8, 9 | V | weak |
107	| RQ5 | Benchmark scores behaviour and appearance only; single-file output means code quality/maintainability is not assessed | 7, 20 | V | weak |
108	
109	Strength note [I]: rows are rated weak because this is a single, non-peer-reviewed benchmark without variance reporting; the IFS < VFS gap is rated moderate because it holds for all 28 models and agrees with the static-vs-interaction gap in [@bai2026recreationworld].
110	
111	## 14. Key quotes
112	> "the best model achieves an overall score of only 36.35%" (p. 1)
113	
114	> "the primary bottleneck for current models is not visual understanding but the synthesis of complex interaction logic" (p. 9)
115	
116	> "Failures in the agent’s evaluation were observed in only three instances." (p. 9)
117	
118	## Analyst notes
119	- Reading coverage: sections read / skipped and why: all 25 PDF pages read via `fulltext.txt`, including appendices A-G (taxonomy, per-dimension tables, metric validation, prompts, case studies). Reference list (p. 11-15) and contributor list (p. 10) skimmed only. Figures (bar chart p. 1, case screenshots p. 22-25) are images and not readable as text; their captions were used.
120	- Uncertainties: (1) runs per model and sampling settings beyond "default" are not reported; (2) whether failed actions stop the replay is not stated; (3) per-category task counts are derived by us from percentages (p. 3), not given directly; (4) we did not check whether the promised data/code release happened; (5) the PDF header says "IWR-Bench Team" and lists contributors on p. 10, consistent with the 21 authors in metadata.json.

598	4.3   Reference and Test-Suite Construction
599	
600	Construction turns a candidate application or website into a reproducible reference and a hidden behav-
601	ioral test suite, together with the inputs required for replay. Figure 4 summarizes the process: prepare the
602	reference, author tests of its observed behavior, and validate the cases before freezing the suite.
603	
604	Reference selection and preparation. Candidates come from open-source desktop repositories, Android
605	projects distributed through GitHub or F-Droid, and openly licensed or benchmark-authored websites.
606	We enforce redistribution requirements and exclude libraries, frameworks, host-program extensions, and
607	applications whose core functionality depends on a login or remote service. Each candidate must run
608	reproducibly in its evaluation environment. Desktop references are pinned to upstream commits, built,
609	and exercised in a graphical session. Android references are built and installed in the emulator, with
610	incidental first-run interruptions removed. Web references are frozen as static snapshots, with pages
611	discovered and reviewed before the scored page set is fixed. We reject references that fail to launch, render
612	incompletely, or lack meaningful interaction. Among the survivors, we balance domains, frameworks,
613	source size, feature complexity, and upstream activity; Web additionally balances real and synthetic sites.
614	Platform-specific selection and preparation details appear in Appendix C.3.
615	
616	Behavioral test authoring. An orchestrator combines source or page analysis with exploration of
617	the running reference to build a shared inventory of features, reachable surfaces, triggering actions,
618	and observable responses. Desktop and Android generators divide this inventory among specialized
619	subagents that author tests for complementary aspects of behavior; depending on the platform’s session
620	constraints, runtime probing is performed by the orchestrator, the subagents, or both. Web uses scripted,
621	agent-authored, interaction, and visual tracks. Each case specifies any required fixture and initial state,
622	an interaction sequence, and programmatic assertions, visual assertions, or both. Source inspection may
623	guide coverage, but assertions depend on runtime-observable behavior rather than reference internals, so
624	the same case can run unchanged against an independent recreation. Figure 8 illustrates this contract
625	through Logbert’s fixed log input, interaction steps, and two assertion channels. Across the frozen suites,
626	81 tasks package 393 files in their fixture trees; this counts packaged files rather than independently
627	addressed test inputs. Web stores its snapshots separately and has no explicit testcase fixture bundle.
628	Appendix C.4 gives the fixture inventory and platform-specific generators.
629	
630	Validation and freezing. We replay every proposed case against a clean reference instance and discard
631	invalid or unstable checks. Uncovered inventory entries guide further authoring, and platform-specific
632	filters prune unsuitable cases, including Web’s discriminativeness and redundancy gates. Human
633	reviewers then inspect each surviving case and its execution on the reference, checking that the fixture,

661	4.4   Evaluation Protocol
662	
663	Evaluation replays each application’s reference-validated hidden suite against the candidate in a clean
664	environment. A fixture is task-supplied data or state installed before replay, such as a document, media
665	file, or directory tree; it is an evaluation input rather than an assertion or expected answer. Each retained
666	case fixes its fixture and initial state, interaction sequence, and expected observations; the same setup is
667	run on the reference and every candidate. The suite freezes two complementary inventories, Prog and
668	VLM, so a candidate cannot change its own denominator. An expected case that is absent, crashes, or is
669	never reached fails, and a candidate that cannot be built or launched receives zero.
670	Prog measures behavior exposed through the platform’s structured automation interface. After replaying
671	the interaction, its assertions read exact text, widget state, navigation, persistence, or computed values
672	through AT-SPI, AXUIElement, UI Automation, or UiAutomator. Desktop and Android score the fraction
673	of frozen cases passed. Web follows the same principle but weights its functional checks by specificity,
674	giving behavior and content greater influence than shallow launch or existence checks.
675	VLM measures rendered behavior at frozen visual checkpoints. The harness pairs each candidate screen-
676	shot with a reference-grounded natural-language assertion, and a shared Qwen3.7-Plus judge (Qwen
677	Team, 2026a) at temperature zero returns a binary verdict. Desktop and Android score the assertion pass
678	fraction; Web first aggregates within each page and viewport, then combines desktop and mobile views
679	across pages. A missing candidate screenshot fails its assertion, whereas a judge transport or parsing
680	failure is an invalid measurement to rerun rather than a model failure.
681	We report Prog and VLM separately, macro-averaging applications within each platform and weighting
682	platforms equally; where a single summary is useful, we average the two channel scores. Figure 8 shows
683	both channels on one Windows case: the same fixture-driven interaction produces exact UI Automation
684	values and a visual checkpoint of the resulting chart.
685	
686	4.5   Isolation and Evaluation Integrity
687	
688	We treat model-generated commands, processes, and artifacts as untrusted. Without isolation, an agent
689	could read reference source code or build artifacts from the local machine, or retrieve the upstream
690	repository from the Internet, reducing reconstruction to source copying. We therefore expose only the
691	running interface, a writable workspace, and necessary tools and inputs, while withholding reference
692	artifacts, hidden evaluation material, and credentials. At handoff, agent-owned processes are terminated
693	and the candidate tree is frozen; a failed isolation check invalidates the run rather than lowering the
694	model’s score.
695	
696	Local permission isolation. Each platform combines a dedicated unprivileged agent principal with
697	POSIX permissions or Windows ACLs, and probes the boundary under that identity before rollout. Only
698	approved fixture copies enter the agent-visible workspace; canonical reference and evaluation assets
699	remain protected. Web necessarily exposes its served client and therefore protects ground truth and
700	tests instead, while Android retains the residual risk that an installed reference package is recoverable in
701	principle. For Web, detected direct repackaging or replay of reference implementation artifacts caps the
702	task aggregate at 0.10; independently authored reconstructions remain permitted. Appendix C.6 gives
703	the complete platform-specific boundaries.

840	6     Analysis
841	
842	To understand how agents approach recreation and where current systems remain limited, we analyze
843	recorded trajectories, delivered source, and evaluator outcomes. Together, these views characterize how
844	agents investigate references, implement and verify their submissions, how the resulting artifacts differ
845	from reference applications, and which tested behaviors most often remain incomplete.
846	
847	6.1     Trajectory-Level Analysis
848	
849	We examine five complementary aspects of the reconstruction process: reference investigation and
850	verification, implementation size over trajectory progress, evaluation-hacking attempts, resource use,
851	and the functional composition of tool calls. Because model identity, harness, and runtime vary together,
852	these comparisons characterize observed workflows but do not isolate the causal effect of any individual
853	behavior.
854	
855	6.1.1    Reference Investigation, Implementation, and Verification
856	Recreation requires an agent to infer the reference’s states and transitions, express that evidence in code,
857	and validate the artifact it will submit. Figure 10 summarizes reference exploration, implementation style,

356	3       Scaling Recreation Environments and Data
357	
358	Recreation requires agents to close the behavioral gap between a running reference and an evolving
359	implementation. Doing so brings active exploration, visual verification, and iterative development into
360	the same long-horizon trajectory, making the resulting experience useful supervision for a broad set of
361	agentic capabilities. Recreation also turns the large and continually refreshed supply of open-source GUI
362	applications and pinned commits into a scalable source of such experience. The executable reference acts
363	as an oracle for constructing behavioral tests, and applying those tests to a candidate provides a direct,
364	implementation-agnostic reward grounded in observable execution rather than annotator preference or
365	source-code similarity. The experiments below test whether training on verified recreation trajectories
366	transfers to coding and hybrid computer-use environments.
367	
368	3.1      Training Setup
369	
370	We source the training tasks from high-quality open-source GUI applications hosted on GitHub and cover
371	the same five platform families as R ECREATION B ENCH. The application pool spans different domains,
372	interface frameworks, programming languages, and levels of behavioral and implementation complexity.
373	This variety exposes agents to different navigation structures, state transitions, and input-dependent
374	behaviors, together with diverse build and runtime requirements. We deduplicate training tasks against
375	the evaluation sets.

379	these rollouts concurrently on isolated workers and records their interaction histories for training. We
380	apply rejection sampling using the task-specific behavioral verifiers to select high-scoring trajectories. We
381	take 7,000 selected trajectories from each platform, yielding a balanced 35,000-trajectory SFT mixture.

598	4.3   Reference and Test-Suite Construction
599	
600	Construction turns a candidate application or website into a reproducible reference and a hidden behav-
601	ioral test suite, together with the inputs required for replay. Figure 4 summarizes the process: prepare the
602	reference, author tests of its observed behavior, and validate the cases before freezing the suite.
603	
604	Reference selection and preparation. Candidates come from open-source desktop repositories, Android
605	projects distributed through GitHub or F-Droid, and openly licensed or benchmark-authored websites.
606	We enforce redistribution requirements and exclude libraries, frameworks, host-program extensions, and
607	applications whose core functionality depends on a login or remote service. Each candidate must run
608	reproducibly in its evaluation environment. Desktop references are pinned to upstream commits, built,
609	and exercised in a graphical session. Android references are built and installed in the emulator, with
610	incidental first-run interruptions removed. Web references are frozen as static snapshots, with pages
611	discovered and reviewed before the scored page set is fixed. We reject references that fail to launch, render
612	incompletely, or lack meaningful interaction. Among the survivors, we balance domains, frameworks,
613	source size, feature complexity, and upstream activity; Web additionally balances real and synthetic sites.
614	Platform-specific selection and preparation details appear in Appendix C.3.
615	
616	Behavioral test authoring. An orchestrator combines source or page analysis with exploration of
617	the running reference to build a shared inventory of features, reachable surfaces, triggering actions,
618	and observable responses. Desktop and Android generators divide this inventory among specialized
619	subagents that author tests for complementary aspects of behavior; depending on the platform’s session
620	constraints, runtime probing is performed by the orchestrator, the subagents, or both. Web uses scripted,
621	agent-authored, interaction, and visual tracks. Each case specifies any required fixture and initial state,
622	an interaction sequence, and programmatic assertions, visual assertions, or both. Source inspection may
623	guide coverage, but assertions depend on runtime-observable behavior rather than reference internals, so
624	the same case can run unchanged against an independent recreation. Figure 8 illustrates this contract
625	through Logbert’s fixed log input, interaction steps, and two assertion channels. Across the frozen suites,
626	81 tasks package 393 files in their fixture trees; this counts packaged files rather than independently
627	addressed test inputs. Web stores its snapshots separately and has no explicit testcase fixture bundle.
628	Appendix C.4 gives the fixture inventory and platform-specific generators.
629	
630	Validation and freezing. We replay every proposed case against a clean reference instance and discard
631	invalid or unstable checks. Uncovered inventory entries guide further authoring, and platform-specific
632	filters prune unsuitable cases, including Web’s discriminativeness and redundancy gates. Human
633	reviewers then inspect each surviving case and its execution on the reference, checking that the fixture,

661	4.4   Evaluation Protocol
662	
663	Evaluation replays each application’s reference-validated hidden suite against the candidate in a clean
664	environment. A fixture is task-supplied data or state installed before replay, such as a document, media
665	file, or directory tree; it is an evaluation input rather than an assertion or expected answer. Each retained
666	case fixes its fixture and initial state, interaction sequence, and expected observations; the same setup is
667	run on the reference and every candidate. The suite freezes two complementary inventories, Prog and
668	VLM, so a candidate cannot change its own denominator. An expected case that is absent, crashes, or is
669	never reached fails, and a candidate that cannot be built or launched receives zero.
670	Prog measures behavior exposed through the platform’s structured automation interface. After replaying
671	the interaction, its assertions read exact text, widget state, navigation, persistence, or computed values
672	through AT-SPI, AXUIElement, UI Automation, or UiAutomator. Desktop and Android score the fraction
673	of frozen cases passed. Web follows the same principle but weights its functional checks by specificity,
674	giving behavior and content greater influence than shallow launch or existence checks.
675	VLM measures rendered behavior at frozen visual checkpoints. The harness pairs each candidate screen-
676	shot with a reference-grounded natural-language assertion, and a shared Qwen3.7-Plus judge (Qwen
677	Team, 2026a) at temperature zero returns a binary verdict. Desktop and Android score the assertion pass
678	fraction; Web first aggregates within each page and viewport, then combines desktop and mobile views
679	across pages. A missing candidate screenshot fails its assertion, whereas a judge transport or parsing
680	failure is an invalid measurement to rerun rather than a model failure.
681	We report Prog and VLM separately, macro-averaging applications within each platform and weighting
682	platforms equally; where a single summary is useful, we average the two channel scores. Figure 8 shows
683	both channels on one Windows case: the same fixture-driven interaction produces exact UI Automation
684	values and a visual checkpoint of the resulting chart.
685	
686	4.5   Isolation and Evaluation Integrity
687	
688	We treat model-generated commands, processes, and artifacts as untrusted. Without isolation, an agent
689	could read reference source code or build artifacts from the local machine, or retrieve the upstream
690	repository from the Internet, reducing reconstruction to source copying. We therefore expose only the
691	running interface, a writable workspace, and necessary tools and inputs, while withholding reference
692	artifacts, hidden evaluation material, and credentials. At handoff, agent-owned processes are terminated
693	and the candidate tree is frozen; a failed isolation check invalidates the run rather than lowering the
694	model’s score.
695	
696	Local permission isolation. Each platform combines a dedicated unprivileged agent principal with
697	POSIX permissions or Windows ACLs, and probes the boundary under that identity before rollout. Only
698	approved fixture copies enter the agent-visible workspace; canonical reference and evaluation assets
699	remain protected. Web necessarily exposes its served client and therefore protects ground truth and
700	tests instead, while Android retains the residual risk that an installed reference package is recoverable in
701	principle. For Web, detected direct repackaging or replay of reference implementation artifacts caps the
702	task aggregate at 0.10; independently authored reconstructions remain permitted. Appendix C.6 gives
703	the complete platform-specific boundaries.

118	1     Introduction
119	
120	General-purpose computer-use agents (CUAs) have advanced along two largely separate lines. One line
121	operates real applications through their graphical interfaces, perceiving screens and issuing clicks and
122	keyboard inputs (Xie et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026); the other works through code and
123	the command line—writing and running programs, invoking build, test, and shell tools, and driving
124	the system through a terminal (Yang et al., 2026a; Jimenez et al., 2024). Each line is blind to what the
125	other does best. A GUI-only agent can observe how a running system behaves but rarely builds or
126	reconfigures the software behind it; a terminal-only agent can author programs and orchestrate tools
127	but cannot see the interface its actions produce, and so has no exploratory visual feedback with which
128	to judge whether the running result matches what was intended. Yet many software-intensive tasks
129	demand both at once: understanding a system requires operating it, while acting on that understanding
130	requires constructing or reconfiguring software. Crucially, they cannot be treated as two stages completed
131	once in sequence. Information must flow back and forth—observations shape the implementation, and
132	running the implementation reshapes what to observe next—so the capability is a genuine fusion rather
133	than a GUI agent and a terminal agent stacked end to end. Existing benchmarks still tend to emphasize
134	one interaction mode, leaving an agent’s autonomous coordination of this loop over long horizons
135	under-measured.
136	We refer to agents that sustain this fusion as hybrid CUAs: agents that interleave interface operation with
137	code and command-line tool use within a single long-horizon process, deciding for themselves when to
138	explore, when to implement, and when to run and verify. Two properties make this capability attractive.
139	First, combining the two modalities widens the agent’s action space to match the environments people
140	actually work in, where progress routinely alternates between operating an application and editing the
141	software that drives it. Second, and more consequentially, the hybrid loop is self-grounding: because the
142	agent builds something it can then run and inspect, every cycle produces concrete execution and visual
143	feedback about its own output—feedback the agent can act on to correct itself within a trajectory, and
144	that, being objective and executable, can be scored and selected to improve the agent across training. This
145	makes hybrid computer use not only a broader capability but a naturally verifiable one, and therefore a
146	promising substrate for self-improvement (Singh et al., 2024).
147	To both measure and cultivate this capability, we introduce R ECREATION W ORLD, a framework built
148	around recreation (Figure 2): given a running reference, an agent must discover its behavior and construct
149	a faithful implementation, with no prescribed workflow. Recreation instantiates the hybrid loop in its
150	purest form—the specification is encountered only by operating the reference, while the deliverable is
151	code that must build and run—so an agent cannot succeed by clicking alone or by coding alone. This
152	process is long-horizon by construction: success requires the agent to carry information across repeated
153	cycles of reference exploration, implementation, candidate execution, visual verification, and revision.
154	Recreation offers two additional advantages as an anchor for hybrid CUAs. It yields an objective, execution-
155	grounded signal: the running reference is an oracle from which hidden behavioral tests can be derived
156	and replayed against any candidate, giving an implementation-agnostic reward that, once the suite is
157	validated and frozen, can be applied without per-candidate human judgment (Wang et al., 2026)—an
158	instance of the asymmetry of verification (Wei, 2025). Recreation is also scalable: the large, continually
159	refreshed supply of open-source applications can be turned into an open-ended stream of tasks and
160	verified trajectories rather than a fixed, hand-authored set (Aggarwal et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026).
161	Concretely, R ECREATION W ORLD provides reproducible application recreation task environments across
162	Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android, and Web, standardizing reference execution, candidate delivery,
163	and experiment logging while preserving each platform’s native interaction semantics. The task pool
164	spans application domains, interface frameworks, implementation languages, and levels of behavioral

172	than variations of a narrow task template. A unified agent harness exposes platform-native GUI control
173	alongside coding tools through a common execution contract, while reference-grounded test generation
174	turns heterogeneous application behavior into comparable, automatically scored outcomes. Together,
175	these components make the same environments useful both for controlled evaluation and for generating
176	diverse, execution-grounded training experience.
177	We run recreation rollouts in task-isolated workers scheduled across a horizontally scalable virtual-
178	machine pool and retain high-scoring trajectories as a shared training set for two model initializations.
179	Across five out-of-distribution benchmarks covering coding, visual coding, and hybrid computer use,
180	both training runs finish above their first evaluated checkpoints, with gains of up to 17.9 percentage
181	points. These results provide initial evidence that recreation supervision transfers beyond the training
182	environment.
183	For held-out evaluation within R ECREATION W ORLD, we introduce R ECREATION B ENCH: 250 tasks—50
184	each on Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android, and Web—spanning heterogeneous UI frameworks, build
185	systems, and accessibility and automation stacks. Reference implementations are withheld where the
186	platform permits. To turn a running reference into a reliable evaluator, we design hidden test cases
187	along two complementary axes: what they observe and how deeply they interact. Programmatic assertions
188	read exact text, widget state, and action outcomes through each platform’s structured accessibility or
189	automation substrate; visual assertions complement them by judging layout, color, canvas content, and
190	other rendered properties absent from that substrate. Beyond observation coverage, each test case couples
191	a trigger with its induced response and spans interaction depths from single-step state changes to multi-
192	hop navigation, persistence, and end-to-end computations, rather than reducing fidelity to an inventory
193	of visible elements. Platform-specific generation and filtering preserve this mix. Every proposed assertion
194	must first pass on the reference and undergo human review before entering the fixed hidden suite, which
195	is then replayed unchanged against the candidate. Together, these choices produce a graded measure of
196	semantic and visual fidelity without constraining the candidate’s language, framework, or architecture.
197	We evaluate ten frontier models on R ECREATION B ENCH and find a substantial gap to reference-level
198	behavioral fidelity. GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest overall score at 58.1% and is the only model with
199	full programmatic passes on multiple platforms, although such passes cover just 2.8% of tasks. Trajectory
200	analysis shows that GUI interaction continues after implementation begins and that GPT-6 Astra combines
201	broad reference exploration with a GUI-centered workflow; these descriptive comparisons do not establish
202	that these behaviors cause higher scores. Across the training sweeps, agents at later checkpoints also
203	check their own rendered outputs more often. Outcome analysis shows that agents reproduce static
204	interface structure more reliably than interactions and computed outputs, while generated applications
205	are substantially smaller and more monolithic than their references. We release R ECREATION B ENCH, its
206	task environments, and test suites to support the study and development of long-horizon hybrid CUAs
207	that jointly reason over interfaces and code.

209	2     R ECREATION W ORLD: Task and Framework
210	
211	2.1   Task Formulation
212	
213	Application recreation asks an agent to construct a runnable application from an executable reference.
214	Each task is defined by three parts: 1) Input. The agent receives a high-level task prompt, interactive
215	access to a running reference application A⋆ , and a prepared environment containing both GUI control
216	and software-development tools; 2) Interaction. The agent may move repeatedly among operating
217	the reference, writing code, building and launching its implementation, and visually and behaviorally
218	checking the running candidate against what it has observed. The task specifies the desired artifact, but
219	not the order or modality of these actions; 3) Output. The agent returns a complete source submission
220	S that satisfies the platform’s build and launch contract: source with build and launch entry points on
221	desktop, a Gradle project producing an APK on Android, or scaffolded source producing a self-contained
222	index.html on the web. Building and launching S produces the runnable candidate application b     A.
223	The submission need not reproduce the reference’s architecture or source structure; only its observable
224	behavior is evaluated. Section 4.4 defines the fidelity measure, while Section 4.1 describes the platform-
225	specific reference visibility boundary.
226	
227	2.2   Why Recreation?
228	
229	Hybrid by necessity. Recreation cannot be completed by operating a graphical interface alone, nor by
230	generating code alone. The specification is encountered through the reference application’s windows,

995	6.1.3                             Hacking Attempts
996	Prior work has observed tool-using agents searching for benchmark materials during evaluation (An-
997	thropic, 2026c). Recreation presents a similar concern: an agent may seek shortcuts through protected
998	information rather than infer the reference’s behavior through GUI exploration. We therefore examine
999	four classes of executable operations: external-network access, protected reference or evaluation-path
1000	access, inspection or extraction of installed reference packages or binaries, and privilege escalation. We
1001	count each executed operation matching one of the four detectors as an attempt. Repeated matches
1002	within one trajectory count separately, whether they succeed, fail, or are blocked. Figure 12 reports mean
1003	attempts per trajectory rather than the fraction of trajectories with at least one attempt. The metric does
1004	not establish successful access, malicious intent, or explicit evaluation awareness.
1005	Across models, GLM-5.3 has the highest platform-balanced mean in every attempt category. Its network-
1006	attempt rate is 1.57× the next-highest rate, and its protected-path rate is nearly twice the next highest.
1007	GPT-6 Astra exhibits a different profile: it ranks second on network attempts but lowest on protected-path
1008	attempts, while package- or binary-directed matches are concentrated in GLM-5.3. These differences
1009	would be obscured by a single aggregate evaluation-hacking statistic. More broadly, agents repeatedly
1010	issue executable operations matching network-egress and protected-path detectors during benchmark
1011	runs. Evaluation integrity therefore cannot rely on prompt compliance alone: prohibited resources
1012	require explicit access controls and auditing. The observed attempts do not imply that any boundary was
1013	successfully bypassed.

1618	
1619	Scalable environments for agentic tasks. Scalable agent training requires diverse executable tasks,
1620	reusable environments, and reliable feedback on outcomes. Gym-Anything (Aggarwal et al., 2026)
1621	automates software setup and auditing, producing long-horizon tasks and trajectories for distillation.
1622	CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026) jointly generates task instructions, environment states, and executable
1623	reward functions, and synthesizes mock web applications to expand its training environment pool. GUI-
1624	GENESIS (Cao et al., 2026) reconstructs real applications as lightweight environments with code-native
1625	rewards, while InfiniteWeb (Zhang et al., 2026), AutoWebWorld (Wu et al., 2026), and VeriEnv (Chae et al.,
1626	2026) synthesize or recreate functional websites with programmatic verification. OSGym (Qin et al., 2026)
1627	addresses the infrastructure cost and reliability of parallel operating-system rollouts. Complementary
1628	efforts scale the experience used to learn agent policies: OpenCUA (Wang et al., 2025b) builds cross-
1629	platform demonstrations and reflective trajectories, while OS-ATLAS (Wu et al., 2024) develops cross-
1630	platform GUI grounding data and action models. UI-TARS (Qin et al., 2025) develops a native GUI
1631	agent with screenshot-based perception, unified action modeling, and iterative training on reflective
1632	interaction traces; UI-TARS-2 (Wang et al., 2025a) extends this line with multi-turn reinforcement learning
1633	and a hybrid GUI–terminal sandbox. ComputerRL (Lai et al., 2025) scales online reinforcement learning
1634	over hybrid API–GUI desktops, and SCALECUA (Lv et al., 2026) couples verifiable task synthesis with
1635	efficient online reinforcement learning. EvoCUA (Xue et al., 2026) combines verifiable task synthesis,
1636	large-scale rollouts, and iterative policy improvement. Qwen-CUA (Lu et al., 2026) scales screenshot-
1637	only native computer use with long-horizon verifiable tasks and also studies Bash-augmented operation.
1638	R ECREATION W ORLD connects scalable task construction, automatic verification, and trajectory generation
1639	within a common framework for agent training and evaluation. Executable references provide behavioral
1640	supervision without prescribing an implementation, while reproducible environments support diverse,
1641	long-horizon experience that can be scored and selected by its outcomes. Our transfer experiments on
1642	
1643	
1644	                                                       20
1645	
1646	=== [PDF page 21] ===
1647	
1648	external coding and computer-use benchmarks provide initial evidence that this experience develops
1649	agent capabilities beyond the source tasks.
1650	
1651	Hybrid computer use. OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) and OSWorld 2.0 (Yuan et al., 2026) evaluate agents
1652	operating desktop applications, while WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) and AndroidWorld (Rawles et al.,
1653	2025) provide web and mobile environments with execution- and state-based evaluation. WeaveBench (Li
1654	et al., 2026b) and PhoneHarness (Li et al., 2026a) explicitly study workflows that coordinate GUI in-
1655	teraction with command-line, code, or structured tool actions. CoAct-1 (Song et al., 2025) delegates
1656	between GUI operation and executable code, whereas StateAct (Yang et al., 2026b) makes program-state
1657	access primary and reserves GUI interaction for visually grounded subgoals. Qwen-UI-Agent (Zhou
1658	et al., 2026) learns mixed GUI and command-line actions across mobile, desktop, and web environments.
1659	EdgeBench (Zhu et al., 2026) measures within-run improvement over day-scale executable tasks, while
1660	Agents’ Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026) evaluates expert-authored professional workflows with verifiable
1661	outcomes. R ECREATION W ORLD focuses on autonomous coordination of the explore–implement–verify
1662	loop: observations inform code and tool use, while executing and inspecting the agent’s own outputs
1663	reveals what to explore or revise next. Its unified GUI–code harness and five-platform benchmark,
1664	R ECREATION B ENCH, provide a reproducible setting for studying this long-horizon coordination across
1665	heterogeneous environments, including whether agents use execution and visual feedback to correct
1666	their own outputs.
1667	
1668	Visual and interactive coding. Visual coding connects visual observations with code generation,
1669	modification, and verification. Design2Code (Si et al., 2025) and DesignBench (Xiao et al., 2025) evaluate
1670	screenshot-conditioned front-end generation, while Web2Code (Yun et al., 2024) and WebCode2M (Gui
1671	et al., 2024) provide large-scale data for visual front-end development. SWE-bench Multimodal (Yang
1672	et al., 2025) extends this scope to bug fixing in visual JavaScript software, with images in problem
1673	statements or unit tests. Interaction2Code (Xiao et al., 2024) extends evaluation to dynamic webpage
1674	interactions, and WebGen-Bench (Lu et al., 2025) evaluates instruction-driven website construction
1675	through agent-executed functional tests. Vision2Web (He et al., 2026) spans static pages, interactive
1676	multi-page frontends, and full-stack development, combining GUI-agent verification with visual judging.
1677	Beyond websites, APPFORGE (Ran et al., 2025) studies Android application development from natural-
1678	language specifications and constructs functional tests by navigating reference applications, followed by
1679	expert verification; RealDevWorld (Bian et al., 2025) evaluates generated software through interactive GUI
1680	testing of function, appearance, and runtime behavior; and GameCraft-Bench (Luo et al., 2026) evaluates
1681	complete game artifacts through executable gameplay and multimodal assessment. These works establish
1682	functional behavior and visual fidelity as complementary evaluation targets. R ECREATION W ORLD
1683	extends visual coding to tasks in which the target must be actively discovered through interaction.
1684	Agents infer visual and behavioral requirements from a running reference, then execute and inspect their
1685	own outputs to guide further exploration and revision. Frozen, reference-validated programmatic and
1686	visual tests score both appearance and action-conditioned behavior, allowing diverse implementations to
1687	be evaluated without prescribing their architecture or the agent’s workflow.
1688	
1689	8   Conclusion and Limitations
1690	We introduced R ECREATION W ORLD, a framework for studying hybrid computer-use agents that must
1691	move repeatedly among GUI exploration, implementation, execution, and verification. Across Ubuntu,
1692	macOS, Windows, Android, and Web, application recreation turns a running reference into both an
1693	interactive specification and a source of automatically scored training experience. Reference-grounded
1694	programmatic and visual tests measure action-conditioned behavior without prescribing the candidate’s
1695	implementation. This combination makes it possible to study the full interface–code loop in reproducible
1696	environments rather than evaluating GUI operation and software construction in isolation.
1697	Using these environments, we selected a balanced set of 35,000 trajectories, with 7,000 from each platform,
1698	to train two model initializations. Both training runs improved from their first evaluated checkpoints
1699	across five out-of-distribution coding and hybrid computer-use benchmarks, with gains of up to 17.9
1700	percentage points, while their trajectories shifted toward more active code and visual verification and
1701	increased GUI interaction. For held-out evaluation, R ECREATION B ENCH contributes 250 applications, 50
1702	per platform. Frontier agents remain well below reference fidelity: interactions and computed outputs
1703	are harder to reproduce than static interface structure, and recreated applications remain smaller and
1704	more structurally concentrated than their references. We release the benchmark, environments, and test
1705	suites to support further work on agents that can use execution feedback to improve what they build.
1706	
1707	Limitations. R ECREATION B ENCH emphasizes pinned, reproducible environments, which limits cov-
1708	erage of workflows involving live services, changing external state, or real-user interaction. Its hidden

1714	
1715	suites sample a finite set of visual and behavioral outcomes, so passing them cannot establish equivalence
1716	across all states and interaction paths. Public reference implementations may also have appeared in
1717	pretraining data, and source-overlap screening cannot rule out prior memorization or all forms of source
1718	reuse. The scores therefore measure fidelity within the specified environments and frozen test suites.
1719	Future work could incorporate controlled online and multi-user workflows, expand hidden-test coverage
1720	across states and interaction paths, and introduce newly constructed references to reduce contamination
1721	risk.

2714	C.7   Agent Harness Details
2715	
2716	Control and recovery. The control servers listed in Table 9 translate model actions into the native
2717	desktop, Android, and browser interfaces and are therefore part of the measurement system. A blocked
2718	operating-system call is bounded before the outer transport timeout, tool-level failures are distinguished
2719	from transport failures, and transient transport or session failures can be retried instead of silently
2720	consuming the remaining trajectory budget.
2721	
2722	Image counting. For the trajectory statistic in Section 6.1.1, we count each image block returned through
2723	a logged tool result: image blocks within Claude Code user messages and input image blocks within
2724	Codex tool outputs. Raw logs may retain the same image in an additional tool-result field; these storage
2725	copies are excluded, while repeated image reads count separately. GLM-5.3 is excluded because its
2726	endpoint does not accept image input.
2727	
2728	Programmable desktop runtime. With direct MCP use, each observation, click, keystroke, or other
2729	primitive returns control to the model and can add another accessibility tree, window description, or inter-
2730	mediate result to its context. Our desktop harness additionally exposes Qwen Code’s qwen-cua-driver
2731	through a typed JavaScript SDK in a session-persistent Node.js REPL. The agent can retain window
2732	handles and helper functions, use loops and conditionals, combine actions with subsequent observations,
2733	and locally filter structured results before returning selected information to the model. This interface
2734	changes interaction granularity without imposing a task-specific sequence or removing access to visual
2735	inspection.
2736	
2737	Separate comparison protocol. We compare direct MCP with the programmable configuration on a
2738	matched set of the 50 Windows applications using Claude Opus 4.8. Task quality uses every evaluator-
2739	valid pair, whereas efficiency metrics use the 39 pairs for which both runs have a non-error terminal
2740	result and complete usage records. The modest change in screenshots entering context, together with
2741	the larger reduction in tool-result text, indicates that the savings primarily come from local aggregation
2742	and selective processing of textual observations rather than less visual inspection. The programmable
2743	path also changes the corresponding driver version and model-facing guidance, and each task has one
2744	rollout, so Figure 9 is an end-to-end configuration comparison rather than an isolated causal estimate of
2745	the persistent runtime.

2750	output comparison. The cases illustrate distinct behaviors without estimating their frequency. Assistant
2751	quotations preserve their original wording; tool results are abridged to relevant fields, with omissions
2752	marked in brackets. Transcript statements are the agent’s own observations, whereas the scores in Table 12
2753	come from the hidden evaluations of the inspected case artifacts.

2715	
2716	Control and recovery. The control servers listed in Table 9 translate model actions into the native
2717	desktop, Android, and browser interfaces and are therefore part of the measurement system. A blocked
2718	operating-system call is bounded before the outer transport timeout, tool-level failures are distinguished
2719	from transport failures, and transient transport or session failures can be retried instead of silently
2720	consuming the remaining trajectory budget.
2721	
2722	Image counting. For the trajectory statistic in Section 6.1.1, we count each image block returned through
2723	a logged tool result: image blocks within Claude Code user messages and input image blocks within
2724	Codex tool outputs. Raw logs may retain the same image in an additional tool-result field; these storage
2725	copies are excluded, while repeated image reads count separately. GLM-5.3 is excluded because its
2726	endpoint does not accept image input.
2727	
2728	Programmable desktop runtime. With direct MCP use, each observation, click, keystroke, or other
2729	primitive returns control to the model and can add another accessibility tree, window description, or inter-
2730	mediate result to its context. Our desktop harness additionally exposes Qwen Code’s qwen-cua-driver
2731	through a typed JavaScript SDK in a session-persistent Node.js REPL. The agent can retain window
2732	handles and helper functions, use loops and conditionals, combine actions with subsequent observations,
2733	and locally filter structured results before returning selected information to the model. This interface
2734	changes interaction granularity without imposing a task-specific sequence or removing access to visual
2735	inspection.

2738	matched set of the 50 Windows applications using Claude Opus 4.8. Task quality uses every evaluator-
2739	valid pair, whereas efficiency metrics use the 39 pairs for which both runs have a non-error terminal
2740	result and complete usage records. The modest change in screenshots entering context, together with
2741	the larger reduction in tool-result text, indicates that the savings primarily come from local aggregation
2742	and selective processing of textual observations rather than less visual inspection. The programmable
2743	path also changes the corresponding driver version and model-facing guidance, and each task has one
2744	rollout, so Figure 9 is an end-to-end configuration comparison rather than an isolated causal estimate of

2318	Web The web corpus is assembled from two sources, both chosen so that the snapshot we ship can
2319	be redistributed. The first is openly licensed sites: real, in-the-wild sites whose front end is published
2320	under a permissive open-source license, such as documentation portals, project and release pages, and
2321	the reference themes shipped with static-site generators. For these, the served copy can be reproduced
2322	from public sources and released as a documented offline derivative with the required notices and
2323	modifications clearly marked. The second is hand-authored synthetic sites: complete multi-page sites that
2324	we design and implement ourselves. Because we author these sites, we can release their code under
2325	MIT and their content and evaluation data under CC-BY-4.0; they also let us cover layout archetypes
2326	and interaction patterns that the first group covers unevenly, including dashboards, product catalogs,
2327	booking and checkout flows, and deep mega-menu navigation. The two groups also differ in what they
2328	contribute: the licensed sites supply the irregularity of real design work, while the synthetic sites give us
2329	structures whose intended behavior we know exactly.
2330	Candidate sites then pass a filter that ends by fixing the scored page set. Page discovery combines a scan of
2331	the snapshot on disk with a JavaScript-disabled breadth-first crawl from the home page, and merges the
2332	two into a page inventory and a navigation graph; the crawl is not bounded by a page budget, so a large
2333	site is enumerated in full rather than truncated at an arbitrary cut-off. Automated screening then browses
2334	every discovered page with a vision-capable agent and rejects it under eight criteria: broken images,
2335	missing stylesheets, empty or never-hydrated content modules, blocking dialogs and authentication
2336	walls, near-duplicate locale variants, pages too thin to carry signal, raw source or feed documents served
2337	in place of a rendered page, and gross render anomalies. Manual review is the authoritative pass: a human
2338	inspects the surviving pages and issues the final verdict, and only a page that clears that review becomes
2339	a scored target. Cascade update propagates the verdicts, dropping rejected pages from the scored set and
2340	regenerating the task definition, so that no ground truth is ever captured for a page we would not score.
2341	The scored set is deliberately narrower than what the agent is asked to build, and the reason is attribution:
2342	every graded page is one a person has confirmed renders correctly from the offline snapshot, so a low
2343	score reflects the recreation rather than a defect in the reference. At the site level we keep only sites that
2344	render deterministically from the offline snapshot and discard those dominated by dynamic feeds or by
2345	media that cannot be captured locally. The home page is never dropped: a site whose home page fails
2346	screening is replaced rather than trimmed, since a task that begins on a broken landing page does not
2347	measure recreation ability.

2349	C.4   Test Generation
2350	
2351	Test specifications are grounded in observations of the running reference rather than expected outcomes
2352	inferred solely from its source. The same specifications are then replayed against the reference and
2353	each recreation, and behavioral fidelity is measured by the recreation’s pass rate over the reference-
2354	validated suite. On Desktop and Android, an orchestrator combines source inspection, which helps
2355	enumerate candidate features and reveal paths, with broad runtime exploration, which supplies the
2356	expected behavior. It records the reachable features, action sequences, and observations in a shared
2357	reconnaissance report and delegates complementary test modules. Whenever behavior can be exercised
2358	reliably, generated tests pair an action with a specific observable outcome; existence checks are retained
2359	only for structural properties that cannot be tested in this way.
2360	Assertions take two forms: programmatic checks that read the accessibility tree directly (a widget’s state,
2361	a label’s text, or the value shown after a sequence of clicks), and visual checks for properties the tree does
2362	not expose (rendered colors, canvas drawing, layout), recorded as a screenshot plus a natural-language
2363	expected state that a vision-language model judges. Every candidate assertion is executed against the
2364	reference before freezing; checks that fail or prove unstable are repaired or discarded, yielding a stable
2365	per-application denominator for scoring.
2366	
2367	Desktop The three desktop platforms use the same six-lane generation scheme: structure, menu, button,
2368	computation, state, and text. The structure lane checks named top-level surfaces and interaction-induced
2369	changes in the accessibility tree; the menu and button lanes exercise safe controls and verify their resulting
2370	dialogs, modes, or displayed values; the computation lane checks observed input–output behavior; the
2371	state lane checks transitions such as checked, enabled, selected, and focused states; and the text lane
2372	checks application-authored labels, status messages, and other content. Assigning each observation to
2373	one lane reduces duplicate scoring, while requiring an action and its observable consequence prevents a
2374	suite from being dominated by widget-existence checks.
