2382	During reconnaissance, the orchestrator records the accessible path to each feature, a safe trigger, the
2383	state before and after the trigger, the navigation path, and any fixture needed to exercise file-dependent
2384	behavior. Source inspection is used to discover features and how to reach them, whereas expected values
2385	and states are taken from the running reference. The generated tests locate controls through platform
2386	accessibility attributes and avoid source-level identifiers or installation paths that need not be preserved
2387	by a faithful recreation. Ubuntu queries the AT-SPI hierarchy by role and accessible name; macOS uses
2388	AXUIElement roles, attributes, and actions; and Windows uses UI Automation through pywinauto,
2389	prioritizing visible names and control types.
2390	The implementations differ primarily in how their desktop sessions constrain generation and validation.
2391	Ubuntu delegates the lanes sequentially because they continue to inspect one shared live application.
2392	The Windows orchestrator also serializes its code-generation lanes, whereas macOS centralizes all
2393	interactive reconnaissance in the orchestrator and parallelizes subagents that only write code, avoiding
2394	concurrent access to its single WindowServer session. Baseline validation then replays every module
2395	on the reference under controlled state: Ubuntu creates a fresh Xvfb, D-Bus/AT-SPI, window-manager,
2396	application, and HOME/XDG environment for each module; Windows performs a cold application
2397	launch per module; and macOS serializes execution in the physical desktop session while launching a
2398	fresh application process and clearing persisted state for every test function. The macOS and Windows
2399	pipelines additionally report the proportions of existence, interactive, value, and multi-surface tests,
2400	together with navigation depth, to expose suites that rely too heavily on shallow static checks.
2401	
2402	Mobile The mobile substrate is the Android UiAutomator view hierarchy, dumped from the running
2403	app after each action and queried by visible text, content description, class, state attributes, and the
2404	package-independent suffix of a resource id. This makes assertions portable across the reference APK
2405	and a recreation installed under a different package name: a test may require the checked state of a
2406	switch, the text of a status label, or the value shown after typing and tapping, but it may not depend on a
2407	source-level identifier, an absolute package prefix, a device path, or a pixel coordinate.
2408	Android instantiates this reference-grounded procedure as six ownership lanes. A structure lane provides
2409	the launch and top-level-surface gate and tree-shape changes; a navigation lane checks surface reachability
2410	and back-stack integrity; an interaction lane checks user-data effects such as CRUD, multi-step sequences,
2411	context menus, and persistence across process death; a computation lane owns input–output value checks;
2412	a state lane owns checked, enabled, selected, and focused transitions together with their app-authored
2413	consequences; and a text lane owns exact strings produced by actions. The ownership split prevents the
2414	same fact from being scored twice and forces every kept case to be a trigger–observation pair rather than
2415	a static enumeration of widgets.
2416	The Android orchestrator first explores the reference app and writes a recon report listing each observed
2417	feature, the action that triggers it, the surface on which it lives, and the observable response. It then
2418	delegates the six lanes to specialized subagents. Each starts from the shared report, actively exercises the
2419	reference within its assigned scope to verify reachable trigger–response pairs, and writes its own module
2420	using a shared read-only runtime kit for adb dispatch, UiAutomator dumps, robust typing, coordinate
2421	refresh, screenshots, VLM calls, and result recording. The six modules emit separate results that are
2422	combined into one fixed, reference-validated suite.
2423	
2424	Web The substrate is the DOM together with the ARIA tree computed over it, queried through Play-
2425	wright by role and accessible name, so an assertion refers to the link named Pricing rather than to a CSS
2426	class or an href. Class names and URL fragments are incidental details that an honest rebuild is free to
2427	choose differently, so selecting on them would penalize faithful work while rewarding a rebuild that
2428	copied the reference markup verbatim.
2429	The specialized generators are organized into four tracks. A scripted track analyzes each reference page
2430	and emits an assertion only when the reference itself satisfies the corresponding condition, so the suite
2431	never requires a property absent from the original site. An agent-authored track has a browsing agent
2432	write the site-specific checks that static analysis cannot anticipate. An interaction track supplies the
2433	depth ≥ 1 assertions that give the functional dimension its discriminative power, dispatching four lanes:
2434	multi-hop routing, dropdown and mega-menu traversal, in-surface tab, accordion and modal interaction,
2435	and mobile hamburger navigation. To distinguish working navigation from a direct scripted visit to
2436	the destination URL, a runtime kit snapshots visible landmarks, headings, and controls as role–name
2437	pairs immediately before and after a real click. The assertion passes only if destination-specific elements
2438	appear and origin-specific elements disappear. A visual track emits the atomic per-page assertions that
2439	the judge of Sec. 4.4 grades, each stating one checkable fact with a required position and concrete color
2440	values, and each judged against the candidate’s screenshot alone.

125	Figure 2: Overview of the IWR-Bench task and evaluation. The inputs to the model are (a) a
126	user interaction video and (b) composite images of all static assets sniffed from the webpage. The
127	evaluation employs an agent-as-judge framework (Zhuge et al., 2024), where an automated agent
128	assesses the rendered page’s interactivity by executing (c) a ground-truth action sequence and its
129	visual fidelity through screenshot comparison.
130	
131	
132	State-of-the-art models can now translate a static screenshot of a webpage into corresponding HTML
133	with impressive fidelity (Yun et al., 2024; Gui et al., 2025). This nascent success, however, highlights
134	a fundamental limitation of current evaluation methodologies. Existing benchmarks are either con-
135	fined to static reconstruction (e.g., Design2Code (Si et al., 2024), WebSight (Laurençon et al., 2024))
136	or model interactions as single-step, stateless events from image pairs (e.g., Interaction2Code (Xiao
137	et al., 2025)), while also failing to provide the necessary static assets for reconstruction. This simpli-
138	fied setup falls short of capturing the continuous, stateful workflows and complete resource context
139	characteristic of real-world web applications. The disconnect between demonstrated capabilities and
140	the demands of true interactivity motivates our central research question: Can LVLMs reconstruct
141	the dynamic, interactive functionalities of a webpage from observing a user interaction video?
142	Reconstructing an interactive webpage from video poses two fundamental challenges. The first,
143	comprehensive multi-modal perception and reasoning (Luo et al., 2024; Gupta & Kembhavi,
144	2023; Song et al., 2025; Deka et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2023), is the process of inferring latent interac-
145	tion logic from dynamic visual evidence. This requires a model to ground its temporal understanding
146	of observed interactions in a precise visual comprehension of the resultant UI states. A critical facet
147	of this reasoning is robust image matching to associate dynamic elements with their static asset
148	counterparts. The second challenge, advanced code generation (Jimenez et al., 2024; Xiao et al.,
149	2025; Li et al., 2022), is the translation of this inferred logic into functional code that implements
150	the complex, stateful logic of interactive applications (e.g., web-games like 2048 and Minesweeper).
151	The construction of a comprehensive benchmark for interactive webpage reconstruction confronts
152	three pivotal challenges. The first pertains to ensuring Diverse Interaction Coverage, which ne-
153	cessitates the curation of tasks spanning a broad spectrum of interaction paradigms and visual com-
154	plexities, while simultaneously adhering to strict standardization for reproducible evaluation. The
155	second challenge centers on the establishment of an Authentic Task Environment. Departing from
156	prior benchmarks characterized by incomplete setups or placeholder assets (Jiang et al., 2025; Gui
157	et al., 2025), this requires the meticulous curation of a complete set of authentic resources from live
158	websites. Such resources must encompass both static assets, such as images and icons, and dynamic
159	content, such as embedded videos, to faithfully represent real-world development contexts. The final
160	challenge lies in the formulation of a Robust Automated Evaluation protocol. Conventional met-
161	rics, including pixel-wise similarity, are insufficient for this purpose (Zhang et al., 2018; Caron et al.,

190	fore employ programmatic interaction with the generated webpage to ascertain both the functional
191	integrity of its components and the state-wise visual consistency across dynamic transitions.
192	This paper formalizes the task of Interactive Webpage Reconstruction (IWR) and introduces IWR-
193	Bench, a comprehensive benchmark that addresses these fundamental design challenges. To ensure
194	comprehensive coverage, tasks are taxonomized along orthogonal axes of application domain, vi-
195	sual complexity, and interaction logic, as illustrated in Figure 3. Each task instance, as depicted in
196	Figure 2, then provides the model with (a) an interaction video that captures a complete, stateful
197	workflow, and (b) the full set of crawled static assets. This setup ensures a realistic reconstruction
198	context. Evaluation is conducted via programmatic interaction: an ‘agent-as-a-judge’ executes a
199	ground-truth (c) action sequence to assess the generated webpage’s functionality. Performance is
200	quantified by two holistic metrics: the Interactive Functionality Score (IFS), a unified measure of
201	operational and logical correctness, and the Visual Fidelity Score (VFS), a composite metric inte-
202	grating low-level features with high-level semantic evaluation.
203	An extensive evaluation on 28 leading LVLMs reveals substantial challenges posed by the IWR
204	task. The top-performing proprietary model, GPT-5, achieves a Final Score of 36.35%. A clear
205	performance hierarchy is observed, as leading open-source models attain lower scores, and video-

213	exists between its functional correctness (24.39% IFS) and visual fidelity (64.25% VFS). This gap
214	indicates a fundamental limitation across the field: while models can reproduce static layouts with
215	moderate success, their capacity for synthesizing event-driven logic remains severely underdevel-
216	oped.
217	Our key contributions are:
218	• A Benchmark for Interactive Webpage Reconstruction. We introduce IWR-Bench, the first
219	  benchmark to formalize and evaluate Interactive Webpage Reconstruction (IWR) from video. It
220	  comprises 113 curated tasks from real-world websites, taxonomized along axes of domain, visual
221	  complexity, and interaction logic.
222	• A Functionality-Centered Automated Evaluation Protocol. We develop a robust evaluation
223	  protocol that employs a programmatic agent to assess functional correctness by executing ground-
224	  truth action sequences. Performance is quantified by two holistic metrics: the Interactive Func-
225	  tionality Score (IFS) and the Visual Fidelity Score (VFS).
226	• An Extensive Evaluation and Analysis. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 28 lead-
227	  ing LVLMs, establishing strong initial baselines. The results reveal a critical performance gap
228	  between visual replication and functional implementation. Further analysis identifies systematic
229	  weaknesses in temporal reasoning and logic synthesis, outlining concrete directions for future
230	  research.
231	
232	2     R ELATED W ORK
233	Webpage Understanding. Webpage understanding evolved from structural analysis based on DOM
234	parsing to a subsequent multimodal perspective that jointly represents a page’s visual and textual
235	content (Furuta et al., 2023; Burns et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a). Large Vision-Language Mod-
236	els (LVLMs) have advanced webpage understanding by enabling a unified approach where a single
237	model demonstrates strong performance across diverse downstream tasks, indicative of deep com-
238	prehension, such as element grounding (Team, 2025) and screen-based question answering (Wang
239	et al., 2024b; Xu et al., 2024). Among these capabilities, generating code from a visual webpage rep-
240	resentation is a key task where existing models have demonstrated strong performance (Beltramelli,
241	2018; Yun et al., 2024; Gui et al., 2025). With the enhanced capabilities of LVLMs in handling
242	multiple images or videos (Bai et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Comanici et al., 2025),
243	a logical extension of this capability is the generation of interactive webpages, moving beyond static
244	layouts to better mimic real-world applications.
245	LVLM Benchmarks. The development of benchmarks for LVLMs has been driven by the rapid ex-
246	pansion of their capabilities, leading to evaluations of increasing complexity (Jimenez et al., 2024;
247	Yang et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023). This progression is evident in the evolution
248	from single-image comprehension to multi-image reasoning and video understanding (Yue et al.,
249	2024; Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024b; Hu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024; Fang
250	et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025; Ning et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025).
251	Concurrently, in the web domain, benchmarks have targeted either webpage understanding or static
252	code generation from a single screenshot (Beltramelli, 2018; Laurençon et al., 2024; Yun et al., 2024;
253	Si et al., 2024; Gui et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Awal et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), with works
254	like IW-Bench (Guo et al., 2024) creating more robust evaluation metrics for this task. A recent
255	advancement, Interaction2Code (Xiao et al., 2025), extends this by generating code from discrete
256	interaction traces. However, such approaches primarily evaluate single-step, stateless events, rather
257	than the complete, stateful workflows captured in continuous video. Therefore, a critical discon-
258	nect exists between model capabilities for dynamic inputs and the benchmarks for interactive web
259	generation.
260	
261	3     IWR-BENCH
262	3.1   TASK D EFINITION AND S TRUCTURE
263	
264	The Interactive Webpage Reconstruction (IWR) task challenges models to generate functional web
265	code from observing user interactions. Formally, given a video V = {f1 , ..., fn } demonstrating user

275	• Video Recording: A screen capture documenting complete user interactions, preserving temporal
276	  dynamics and state transitions that define the webpage’s behavior.
277	• Static Web Assets: All relevant images, icons, and videos necessary for reconstruction. To pre-
278	  vent models from leveraging prior knowledge based on semantic filenames (e.g., logo.png), all

282	  type ai , parameters pi , a natural language description di , a visual evaluation flag vi , and logical
283	  assertions li for verification.
284	• Checkpoint Screenshots: Stable-state images S = {s1 , ..., sk } capturing the visual state after
285	  each action. This ensures evaluation occurs on fully rendered pages rather than on transitional
286	  states.

395	
396	As detailed in Table 2, IWR-Bench addresses a critical gap between webpage reconstruction and
397	video understanding benchmarks. Existing webpage reconstruction benchmarks either focus on
398	static image-to-code tasks (e.g., Pix2Code, WebSight) or model interaction as stateless, single-step
399	events without providing the necessary static assets for reconstruction (e.g., Interaction2Code). Con-
400	versely, general video understanding benchmarks (e.g., MVBench) are designed for comprehension
401	tasks like Video QA, not code generation. IWR-Bench overcomes these limitations by using videos
402	of stateful, full-trajectory workflows from live websites. It provides all required assets and employs
403	a robust agent-based protocol to evaluate true interactive correctness.

407	4.1    E VALUATION P ROTOCOL
408	
409	The evaluation of generated code C is conducted using a deterministic executor built upon the
410	browser-use library (browser-use, 2025). This executor programmatically interacts with the ren-
411	
412	
413	                                                                6
414	
415	=== [PDF page 7] ===
416	
417	dered webpage by sequentially executing each pre-defined action ai from the ground-truth action
418	trajectory T . This design isolates the evaluation to code execution and removes any dependency on
419	high-level task planning, thereby ensuring a stable and reproducible protocol.
420	The evaluation of the trajectory proceeds step-by-step. At each step i, the action ai is attempted. The
421	action is considered a failure under two conditions: (1) it is operationally infeasible (e.g., a target
422	element is not found), or (2) its corresponding logical assertions li are not satisfied.
423	For logical assertion verification, an MLLM judge, specifically Gemini-2.5-Pro (Comanici et al.,
424	2025), is employed to analyze screenshots of the page state before and after an action to determine
425	its correctness. The prompt for this judge is detailed in Appendix E. Upon the successful completion
426	of an action, a new screenshot is captured. If the visual evaluation flag vi for this step is true, the new
427	screenshot undergoes a visual fidelity assessment. This assessment is based on a composite score
428	that integrates OCR-based text similarity (Cui et al., 2025), DINO-based structural similarity (Oquab
429	et al., 2023), and a high-level evaluation also conducted by Gemini-2.5-Pro (see Appendix E for
430	the prompt). Actions where vi is false, which typically involve insignificant or stochastic visual
431	changes, are omitted from this visual assessment phase.

435	Model performance is quantified through a hierarchy of metrics designed to measure functional
436	correctness, visual fidelity, and overall task completion.
437	
438	Interactive Functionality Score (IFS). This metric measures a model’s ability to generate func-
439	tionally correct code. An action ai from the trajectory T is considered successful if and only if
440	it executes without operational errors and all associated logical assertions li are satisfied, as deter-
441	mined by the protocol in Section 4.1. The IFS is defined as the ratio of successfully completed
442	actions (Nsucc ) to the total number of actions (Ntotal ).

448	This score is computed exclusively over checkpoints that were successfully reached and have the
449	visual evaluation flag enabled (vi = true). Let Iv,succ be the set of indices for these qualifying
450	checkpoints. The score for each checkpoint i ∈ Iv,succ is a weighted combination of two compo-

452	DINO-based cosine similarity, and a High-level Visual Score (SHVS,i ), which is a holistic assessment
453	from the MLLM judge. The final VFS is the macro-average of these checkpoint scores. The weight
454	w is set to 0.5 based on validation studies (Section 5.4).

526	Implementation Details. For each task in IWR-Bench, models are provided with the user inter-
527	action video and a composite image of all crawled static assets. To accommodate models without
528	native video support, each video is sampled at 1 fps, with the number of frames capped at 64.

531	generate a single, self-contained HTML file that integrates all necessary CSS and JavaScript to repli-
532	cate the observed webpage. All other inference parameters utilize the default settings recommended
533	by the model providers. The complete prompt templates are detailed in Appendix E.

573	5.3   P ERFORMANCE A NALYSIS ACROSS TASK D IMENSIONS
574	
575	A fine-grained analysis (detailed in Appendix B) reveals distinct performance patterns. The synthe-
576	sis of event-driven functionality is the primary bottleneck, evidenced by a sharp performance drop
577	from static (L1) to interactive (L2-L4) tasks (Table 4). Models also struggle with highly structured
578	layouts (Table 5). Performance varies by domain, with relative strength in ”Entertainment & Media”
579	(Table 6), pointing to structured code generation and state management as key research directions.
580	
581	5.4   VALIDATION OF THE E VALUATION P ROTOCOL
582	
583	The robustness and reliability of the evaluation protocol are validated through a rigorous, two-part
584	analysis that addresses both the metric parameters and the agent-as-a-judge methodology (Zheng
585	et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2025; Maaz et al., 2023). First, the weighting coefficients (w and α) for the
586	scoring metrics are determined through a human alignment study, with the detailed procedure and re-
587	sults presented in Appendix C. Second, the agent-as-a-judge framework is validated through a multi-
588	stage process. This process includes a meticulous cross-verification of annotated action trajectories
589	(Section 3.2), automated verification of logical assertions using an MLLM-based judge(Comanici
590	et al., 2025), and manual inspection of the agent’s operational fidelity. For the manual inspection,
591	three PhD students observed the agent’s execution on 100 randomly sampled, model-generated web-
592	pages, with the browser’s headless mode disabled to compare on-screen behavior against evaluation
593	logs. Failures in the agent’s evaluation were observed in only three instances. These issues typically
594	stemmed from ambiguous element descriptors (e.g., buttons with identical names), which required
595	a more precise locator (d i). All identified discrepancies were subsequently rectified.
596	
597	6     C ONCLUSION
598	This paper introduces IWR-Bench, the first benchmark designed to evaluate Interactive Webpage
599	Reconstruction from video. Through an automated agent-as-a-judge evaluation protocol, perfor-
600	mance is quantified using two metrics: the IFS and the VFS. Comprehensive evaluations on 28
601	LVLMs reveal a stark disparity between visual replication and functional implementation. While
602	models achieve moderate success in reconstructing static appearance (VFS), their ability to generate
603	correct, event-driven logic remains critically limited, as shown by low IFS scores across the board.
604	This finding indicates that the primary bottleneck for current models is not visual understanding but
605	the synthesis of complex interaction logic. IWR-Bench thus establishes a challenging new frontier
606	for vision-language research, highlighting the need for future work to focus on temporal reasoning,
607	dynamic asset binding, and robust code synthesis to create truly functional web applications.

898	A    M ULTI -D IMENSIONAL TASK TAXONOMY
899	To move beyond a monolithic view of difficulty and enable a fine-grained analysis of model capabil-
900	ities, we developed a three-dimensional taxonomy to classify each task. This taxonomy categorizes
901	tasks along the orthogonal axes of Interaction Complexity, Visual Complexity, and Application Do-
902	main, providing a structured framework to understand the specific challenges inherent in each task
903	and to diagnose model failure modes with high precision.
904	
905	Interaction Complexity (L1-L4) This first axis categorizes tasks based on the depth of logical
906	and temporal understanding required for successful reconstruction.
907	      • L1: Static Content Consumption. Tasks involve passive information consumption, pri-
908	        marily requiring correct handling of vertical scrolling to reconstruct long pages that extend
909	        beyond a single viewport (e.g., browsing a blog post or a project’s README).
910	      • L2: Simple State Manipulation. Tasks feature components that manage local state, such
911	        as filtering e-commerce results, switching between on-page tabs, or expanding/collapsing
912	        accordion menus. This level tests the generation of basic client-side event handlers.
913	      • L3: Complex Workflow Interaction. These tasks involve multi-step, sequential inter-
914	        actions where state is passed between components, such as a multi-step product config-
915	        urator or an online booking process. This tests understanding of application logic and
916	        inter-component communication.
917	      • L4: Algorithmic/Game Logic. The most complex level requires the model to reverse-
918	        engineer and implement a set of rules or algorithms, such as an online calculator, a text-
919	        based puzzle, or a simple game like 2048.
920	
921	Visual Complexity (V1-V4) This second axis captures the static challenge of rendering the web-
922	page’s appearance, focusing on its layout and styling.
923	      • V1: Minimalist Layouts. Simple, single- or two-column structures with standard element
924	        alignment, typical of documentation or text-heavy sites.
925	      • V2: Standard Grid-based Layouts. Organized grid systems are used in e-commerce or
926	        news portals, featuring numerous but regularly arranged elements.
927	      • V3: Asymmetric & Modern Layouts. Visually-driven designs with complex CSS, such
928	        as overlapping elements, parallax scrolling, and non-standard component shapes.
929	      • V4: Data-Dense Layouts. Dashboards or admin panels with a high density of information
930	        presented in charts, tables, and data cards, testing the ability to generate precise, repetitive
931	        structures.
932	
933	Application Domain To ensure our benchmark reflects the breadth of real-world web applications,
934	the third axis classifies tasks by their Application Domain. Drawing inspiration from established
935	taxonomies in web-centric agent research (Gou et al., 2025), we group tasks into five high-level
936	domains: Commerce & Services (e-commerce, booking, finance), Knowledge & Education (aca-
937	demic sites, news portals, documentation), Productivity & Tools (calculators, project management
938	boards), Entertainment & Media (games, streaming platforms), and Lifestyle & Community (so-
939	cial forums, blogs). This classification guarantees that models are evaluated across a diverse spec-
940	trum of functionalities and visual paradigms. For instance, a task involving filtering products on an
941	e-commerce site is tagged as [L2, V2, Commerce], while a task requiring the reconstruction of a
942	simple browser game is tagged as [L4, V1, Entertainment]. This multi-dimensional labeling allows
943	us to analyze whether a model’s performance correlates with certain types of interactions, visual
944	styles, or application contexts.

997	C    M ETRIC PARAMETER VALIDATION
998	
999	The VFS and Final Score metrics rely on the weighting coefficients w and α. These parameters are
1000	determined and validated through a human alignment study. A sample of 60 evaluation instances
1001	is constructed by selecting outputs from three randomly chosen models for each of 20 randomly
1002	selected tasks from IWR-Bench. Each instance is assessed by five PhD-level students on two di-
1003	mensions: visual fidelity and overall quality. To determine the optimal parameters, a grid search
1004	is performed over the discrete set {0.1, 0.2, . . . , 0.9} for both w and α. The value that maximizes
1005	the Spearman’s ρ correlation between the automated scores and the aggregated human judgments is
1006	selected. For the VFS metric, the peak correlation (ρ = 0.57) is observed at w = 0.5, indicating an
1007	equal weighting between LVS and HVS. For the Final Score, the maximum correlation with human
1008	overall judgment (ρ = 0.65) is achieved with α = 0.7, empirically validating the decision to weigh
1009	functionality (IFS) more heavily than visual fidelity (VFS).
1010	
1011	D    TASK AND ACTION R EPRESENTATION
1012	
1013	Each task in IWR-Bench is formally defined by an ‘action sequence‘, a structured list of discrete
1014	actions that an automated agent must perform to validate the reconstructed webpage. This rep-
1015	resentation standardizes the evaluation process. We defined a vocabulary of atomic actions, in-
1016	cluding Click(description), Type(key, description), Scroll(direction, amount, description), and
1017	Press(key, description). A crucial design choice is the use of a natural language ‘description‘ field
1018	for targeting elements instead of unstable positional coordinates (e.g., ”Click the primary ’Submit’
1019	button” instead of ”Click at (x:120, y:350)”). This makes the evaluation robust to minor layout vari-
1020	ations in the generated code and tests a more semantic understanding of the page structure, both for
1021	the model during generation and the agent during evaluation.

1138	Case 1 Analysis: E-commerce Workflow Simulation. Our first case study, classified as [L2, V2,
1139	E-commerce], simulates a fundamental e-commerce user journey to test a model’s ability to handle
1140	sequential state manipulations within a standard visual structure. The task requires the model to
1141	replicate a workflow involving filtering a product grid by a specific brand, sorting the filtered results
1142	by price and adding a selected item to the shopping cart.
1143	As illustrated in Figure 8, this task effectively exposes different failure modes in different models.
1144	On the left, Claude-Sonnet-4 demonstrates good capabilities in static replication and simple state
1145	management. It accurately renders the initial layout and correctly implements the action for filtering
1146	and sorting. However, its failure occurs at the final ”add to cart” step. The right side shows the result
1147	of GPT-5. This case likely involved too many static resources, causing the product list on the initial
1148	page to fail to render successfully. By pinpointing these different stages of failure, the benchmark
1149	provides a granular diagnosis of each model’s specific strengths and weaknesses in front-end code
1150	generation.
1151	
1152	
1153	Case 2 Analysis: Algorithmic Logic Reconstruction. This case study moves to the highest level
1154	of our interaction complexity scale, L4, to assess a model’s capacity for algorithmic reasoning.
1155	Classified as [L4, V2, Gaming], the task requires the model to reverse-engineer and implement the
1156	complete set of rules for a simple browser game (e.g., 2048) based solely on observing its behavior in
1157	the input video. The visual complexity is simple (V2), deliberately shifting the evaluation focus from
1158	layout replication to the correctness of the underlying algorithmic logic. The The core challenge is
1159	to deduce and codify the game’s state-transition functions, including tile movement, merging logic,
1160	and the spawning of new tiles.

# Critical review, batch C (2026-11-12)

Project: 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding
Keys reviewed: bai2026recreationworld, xiong2026propgen, chen2025iwr
Reviewer: critical-review subagent. No `analysis.md` was edited.

## Checks run

| Check | bai2026recreationworld | xiong2026propgen | chen2025iwr |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rlab validate` | could not run: `pdftotext not found` (poppler missing on this machine) | same | same |
| metadata.json verification | verified (OpenAlex), identity "arXiv id printed in PDF", not retracted | verified (OpenAlex), identity "DOI printed in PDF", not retracted | verified (arXiv), identity "arXiv id printed in PDF", not retracted |
| Preprint flag | preprint, flagged in the analysis | published (ASE '26). PDF is arXiv v2 with the camera-ready header. Correctly described | preprint, flagged in the analysis |
| Published version | Crossref search 2026-11-12: none found | n/a | Crossref search 2026-11-12: none found |
| `rlab cite-check` | OK (101 citations) | OK (77 citations) | OK (69 citations) |
| RQ ids exist in RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md | yes (RQ1-RQ5) | yes | yes |

Because `rlab validate` failed for a tooling reason, PDF identity could not be re-confirmed in this review. It rests on the recorded `fulltext.identity` field. Install poppler and re-run `rlab validate` before these analyses are marked `complete`.

Items spot-checked against `fulltext.txt`: bai, 31 numbers (Tables 2, 3, 4, 11, 12; pp. 9, 11-18, 28-31, 38-39, 46-47). xiong, 26 (Tables 1-5, kappas, costs, RQ4 counts). chen, 30 (Tables 1, 3-6, Appendix C, prompts).

Answers to the analyst's flagged points:
- **chen per-category counts**: the arithmetic is right (7.96% x 113 = 9.0; 10.62% x 113 = 12.0) and it is labelled [I]. Fine as is. See C1 for a bigger problem with the same tables.
- **bai 13.64% implies 44 tasks**: labelled [I], which is correct. 6/44 is not the only possible fraction (3/22 also gives 13.64%). Add the supporting evidence the paper does give (B4).
- **bai scrape penalty on case scores**: this can be resolved further than the analysis says. Ablira was *detected* (p. 47), yet its reported channel scores (72.73/40.79) are far above the 0.10 cap, so the case table shows pre-penalty channel scores (B3).
- **xiong kappas**: 0.91 / 0.82 / 0.81 match p. 7 exactly. The column interleaving did not garble them.
- **83.8%**: this figure is in **bai**, not xiong (p. 15-16, "83.8% place a larger share of source in the single largest file"). It is correct. The xiong analysis contains no 83.8% figure.

---

## bai2026recreationworld — verdict: **needs-fixes** (10 fixes)

**B1 (serious, factual error). §7 Key finding 1.**
- Current: "Grok 4.6 is lowest (9.15) — [V] (p. 11)".
- Problem: the column headers of Table 3 are scrambled in the text layer. The column with 9.18 / 9.12 / 9.15 is **Qwen3.7-Plus**, not Grok 4.6. Evidence:
  - Figure 1 (p. 1) lists the models in descending five-platform mean: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, **Grok 4.6**, Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Kimi K3, Claude Opus 4.8, GLM-5.3, Gemini 3.7 Flash, **Qwen3.7-Plus**.
  - The scaffold labels in Figure 1 match Table 8 (p. 28): Grok xhigh, Qwen3.7-Plus "enabled".
  - Read in that order, the Table 3 averages are strictly descending: 58.06, 44.16, 42.06, 36.73, 34.80, 31.41, 31.10, 24.38, 21.12, 9.15.
- Correct text: "...then Claude Opus 5 (44.16) and GPT-5.6 Sol (42.06); Grok 4.6 is fourth (36.73) and Qwen3.7-Plus is lowest (9.15) — [V] (p. 1, p. 11)."
- Knock-on edit to §9 COI: "[I] Qwen3.7-Plus, which is also the VLM judge (p. 9), is the lowest-scoring evaluated model (VLM 9.12, average 9.15, p. 11). So no favourable self-scoring is visible, but judge self-preference was not tested."

**B2 (serious, scope). §7 findings 4, 5, 7; §12; §13 RQ3 rows.**
- Current: "Rebuilt apps are much smaller... 89.4%...", "Claude Opus 5 has the highest median recreation LOC on all five platforms, while GPT-6 Astra has the lowest on four of five", "final edit -> relaunch -> inspect ... 23.6-47.5% of trajectories". All are presented as general findings.
- Problem: the trajectory and artifact analyses cover only **4 of the 10 models**: Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GLM-5.3 and Qwen3.8-Max-0902 (Figure 10 legend p. 12; "for the four models analyzed above", p. 15).
  - The reference-size comparisons cover native platforms only (p. 15).
  - "Coverage varies across model–platform cells" (p. 15), and the denominators are not given.
  - "Highest/lowest LOC" therefore means highest/lowest among four models.
- Correct text: add to findings 4, 5 and 7, and to the RQ3 evidence rows: "(four models analysed: Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max-0902; desktop and Android only for reference comparisons; per-cell coverage not reported) (p. 12, p. 15)". In finding 5: "...the highest median recreation LOC **among the four analysed models**...".

**B3 (serious, misreported integrity evidence). §7 finding 8; §9 "Score integrity gap"; §13 RQ4 row "scraped-content replay can earn substantial scores"; Analyst notes uncertainty (4).**
- Current: "Two Web cases replayed scraped reference content yet scored 72.73% and 54.82% Prog, one escaping the detector"; "whether the 0.10 scrape cap (p. 38) was applied to those reported case scores ... is not reported".
- Problem: the paper says the detector **caught** Ablira ("source-level class-provenance and scrape-mechanism checks catch Ablira's bulk replay", p. 47). A SCRAPE verdict replaces the task aggregate with min(s, 0.10) (p. 9, p. 38).
  - Ablira's reported 72.73 Prog / 40.79 VLM (p. 39, p. 46) are therefore pre-penalty channel scores. Its penalised aggregate would be at most 0.10. This is [I], but it follows directly from the stated rule.
  - Only Kartova (54.82 Prog / 14.63 VLM / 34.72 average, p. 47), which escaped the detector, shows a replay that kept a real score.
  - As written, the RQ4 row overstates the integrity gap.
- Correct text, finding 8: "Two Web case studies replayed reference content. Ablira (72.73% Prog / 40.79% VLM, p. 46) was caught by the scrape detector, so the 0.10 aggregate cap applies (p. 38, p. 47); the table shows its pre-penalty channel scores [I]. Kartova escaped detection and kept 54.82% Prog / 14.63% VLM (34.72% average) (p. 47) — [V]."
- RQ4 row: "A transformed replay evaded the scrape detector and scored 54.82% Prog (p. 47); detected replay is capped at 0.10 (p. 38) | 38, 46, 47 | V | weak". Update analyst note (4) to match.

**B4 (moderate, unsupported inference needs its evidence). §9 "Unexplained denominators"; Analyst notes (3).**
- Current: "13.64% (p. 30), consistent with 6 of 44 rather than 50 tasks, suggesting some runs were excluded as invalid".
- Problem: the [I] label is right, but the inference skips an alternative and leaves out the support the paper gives.
  - 13.64% equals 6/44 and also 3/22. With 50 tasks, every value would be a multiple of 2.00, as all other cells in Table 11 are (p. 30).
  - The paper states that a failed isolation check "invalidates the run rather than lowering the model's score" (p. 9). Quality metrics use "evaluator-valid" pairs (p. 11, p. 38), and the paired Bash comparison covers "249 application–platform pairs" (p. 20). So exclusions exist, but their number is never reported.
- Correct text: "[I] Claude Opus 5's Web Prog >= 90% of 13.64% (p. 30) cannot come from 50 tasks; it fits 6/44 (or 3/22). The paper invalidates runs that fail isolation checks (p. 9) and reports evaluator-valid subsets elsewhere (p. 11, p. 20), so some runs were probably excluded. The number of excluded runs per model and platform is not reported."

**B5 (moderate, missed evidence on run count). §5 "Rollouts per task per model in the main benchmark: not reported"; §9 "No variance"; frontmatter `sample_size`.**
- Problem: the statement is literally true, but the paper gives indirect evidence. The direct-MCP arm of the Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 comparison is "one rollout per task" (p. 11, p. 38). Its scores (Prog 35.05, VLM 31.00, Figure 9, p. 11) are identical to the Table 11 Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 entries (35.05 / 31.00, p. 30).
- Correct text (add to §5 and §9): "[I] The main benchmark is probably a single rollout per task. The one-rollout direct-MCP arm (p. 11) reproduces the Table 11 Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 scores exactly (p. 30). This is not stated explicitly."

**B6 (moderate, missing appraisal of the transfer experiment). §7 finding 9; §9; §12.**
- Problem: the analysis records the authors' "exploratory" caveat but does not appraise the design.
  - Gains are measured against "each run's first evaluated checkpoint", not the untrained initialisation (p. 3, p. 6).
  - There is no control arm, such as SFT on equally long non-recreation agent trajectories, so the effect of recreation data cannot be separated from any SFT on agentic trajectories.
  - Each OOD benchmark is run once per task per checkpoint (p. 6, p. 28).
  - Curves are non-monotonic (p. 6), and the gain reported is the last-vs-first difference, with no uncertainty.
- Correct text, new §9 bullet: "[I] **Transfer design is uncontrolled.** Improvements are measured from the first evaluated checkpoint (p. 6), with one trial per task (p. 28) and no control SFT mixture. Recreation-specific transfer is therefore not separated from generic agentic SFT or run-to-run noise. 'Gains up to 17.9 points' (p. 3) is a single best-case difference."

**B7 (labels). §13 evidence table.**
- Rows labelled V that are our appraisal of absences or confounds:
  - "RQ4 | No CIs or repeated runs for main scores; judge accuracy and reviewer agreement not reported; model and scaffold confounded"
  - "RQ5 | ... maintainability ... assessed only through size and structure proxies"
- Required: label both **I**, with the basis (p. 11, p. 28; p. 15-16). The paper does not state the RQ5 proposition. The authors' own framing ("architectural substitution rather than implementation quality", p. 16) can be cited as [A].

**B8 (hedging of the cross-paper claim). §12 "The interaction-vs-appearance pattern agrees with [@chen2025iwr]".**
- Problem: in bai the aggregate VLM (visual) channel is *not* higher than Prog. GPT-6 Astra has VLM 57.92 vs Prog 58.19, and several models have VLM below Prog (Claude Opus 5 42.34 vs 45.99) (p. 11). The bai support comes from category pass rates *within* the programmatic channel (structure vs action-conditioned, p. 16-17), not from a visual-vs-functional channel gap like chen's VFS vs IFS.
- Correct text: "[I] Directionally consistent with [@chen2025iwr]. Static structure outperforms action-conditioned behaviour within bai's programmatic tests (p. 16-17), but bai's visual channel does not exceed its programmatic channel in aggregate (p. 11). The two papers measure the gap differently."

**B9 (minor, missing reliability caveat). §9 "Web scores are panel-relative".**
- Fine as [I]. Add that the panel's composition is not reported, and that the gate runs on "rebuilds from a panel of models" (p. 34). If those models overlap with the evaluated ones, Web scores are partly defined by the evaluated models themselves.

**B10 (minor, paper-internal inconsistency worth recording). Analyst notes.**
- Table 12 (p. 39) lists a case "GLM-5.2 / Ubuntu", but GLM-5.2 is not among the evaluated models in Table 8 (p. 28), which lists glm-5.3. Note it as a paper inconsistency that is not resolvable from the text.

Checked and correct: findings 2, 3, 6, 7 (numbers), 8 (overlap table), 10. Also the 20-hour budget, 35,000 trajectories, 81 tasks / 393 fixtures, the 0.10 cap rule, the coverage audit (77% / 24% / 94.2% / 40.7%), the judge model and temperature, the licence breakdown, and all three key quotes (verbatim). The limitations in §8 are all stated by the authors on the cited pages.

---

## xiong2026propgen — verdict: **pass-with-minor-fixes** (5 fixes)

**X1 (moderate, understated bias). §9 "Possible author-tool bias".**
- Current: "Kea and PBFDroid come from overlapping author groups (refs [52], [71], p. 12-13) ... consulting the original tool authors partly mitigates this."
- Problem: the overlap is wider than stated, and the mitigation is weaker.
  - PropGen co-author Ting Su is an author of Genie [51], Odin [63], PBFDroid [52], Kea [71] and Kea2 [29].
  - Yiheng Xiong co-authored Genie [51] and Kea [71], and Bo Ma co-authored Kea2 [29] (p. 12-13).
  - Three of the four RQ4 baselines (Genie, Odin, PBFDroid; p. 7) therefore come from the PropGen authors' own group. "We further consulted the authors of Genie, Odin, and PBFDroid" (p. 8) partly means consulting a co-author of this paper.
- Correct text: "[I] **Author-tool overlap.** Ting Su (PropGen co-author) co-authored Genie, Odin, PBFDroid and Kea; Xiong co-authored Genie and Kea (refs [29], [51], [52], [63], [71], p. 12-13). The scope analysis is manual (p. 8), its 'validation' by the baseline authors involves the same group, and the PBFDroid properties were written by the PropGen authors (p. 8). Only VisionDroid (p. 7) is independent. This is not necessarily bias in PropGen's favour, since the group knows these tools well, but the scope analysis is not independently validated."

**X2 (moderate, framing that matters for our RQs). §12 "it recovers behavioural specifications from a running black-box app (no source, no spec)"; also the RQ2 evidence row "...from a running Android app without specs".**
- Problem: PropGen is not purely observational.
  - It feeds the MLLM "the list of activity names extracted from the AndroidManifest.xml file" (p. 4).
  - It filters widget text against "a whitelist extracted via static analysis" (p. 5).
  - "Black-box" is the authors' description (p. 11) and should be labelled [A].
  - For a reverse-engineering study, this is observation plus static analysis of the APK (grey-box).
- Correct text: "...recovers behavioural specifications from a running app without source code or written specifications, using runtime observation plus light static analysis of the APK (manifest activity names, a string whitelist; p. 4-5). The authors call this 'exploring a black-box app' [A] (p. 11)."

**X3 (moderate, one-sided evidence row). §13 RQ2 row "Generated properties found 25 previously unknown functional bugs in 12 apps; prior tools rediscovered only 3".**
- Problem: this leaves out the opposite direction, which the paper reports alongside it: the four prior tools together found 13 unknown bugs, 10 of which PropGen missed (p. 10).
- Correct text: "...prior tools rediscovered 3 of them, but themselves found 13 unknown bugs, 10 of which PropGen missed; authors call the approaches complementary [A] (p. 10)."

**X4 (minor, missing appraisal). §9.**
- Add "[I] Whether the annotators were blind to which tool (PropGen or DroidAgent) produced each functionality is not reported (p. 7). The set of items over which Cohen's kappa was computed (PropGen only, or both tools) is not stated (p. 7)."

**X5 (minor, label). Frontmatter `sample_size` "single run each"; §6 "single run per tool and app (p. 8-10)"; §13 RQ4 row "Single run per tool and app ... | 7, 8 | V".**
- Problem: the paper says "This single run" only for the RQ4 prior techniques (p. 8). For PropGen's RQ1-RQ3 no repetition is reported, but "single run" is not stated either.
- Correct text: "No repeated runs are reported (single run stated for RQ4 baselines, p. 8)". Label the evidence row **I**.

Checked and correct:
- Every number in §7 against Tables 2-5 (pp. 8-10) and the text: 1,282 / 1,210 / 977; 575 / 491 / 187; 985 / 912 (78.7-98.8% per app); 240 / 0; 127 / 118 with 53 / 1 / 64; 9 = 5 + 4; 25 bugs = 12 + 6 + 4 + 3; 7 (28%) / 3 (12%); 13 and 10.
- Costs; kappas 0.91 / 0.82 / 0.81; GPT-5.2 snapshot and temperature; budgets of 3 h + 6 h and 9 h; Zenodo DOI; funding; received/accepted dates; all three quotes.
- Two-column interleaving did not corrupt any number used. §8 limitations are all author-stated (p. 9-11).

---

## chen2025iwr — verdict: **needs-fixes** (9 fixes)

**C1 (serious, misread metric). §7 finding 5; §13 RQ2 row "Functional fidelity falls from static to algorithmic tasks (GPT-5 Final 61.85 on L1 vs 25.26 on L4)".**
- Problem: Tables 4-6 report **Final Score only** ("For each task category, the Final Score is reported", p. 16). They are not IFS, and Table 5 is not a visual score.
  - "Functional fidelity falls" and "Data-dense layouts (V4) are hardest visually" misdescribe what was measured.
  - The pattern is also not monotonic. For GPT-5, L2 and L3 are nearly equal (35.43 vs 35.12). Several models score L3 above L2: Claude-Sonnet-4 32.86 vs 31.04, Claude-Opus-4 (thinking) 32.57 vs 31.52, GPT-4.1 31.98 vs 30.32 (p. 17). For GPT-5, V3 is well above V2 (43.77 vs 30.73, p. 18). The robust contrast is L1 vs the rest.
  - L1 ("Static Content Consumption", mainly scrolling, p. 16) has about 9 tasks [I].

## Cross-paper observations

1. **"Looks right, behaves wrong" is claimed as convergent evidence in both §12s, but the two papers measure different things** (see B8, C2, C7).
   - chen: VFS vs IFS, where VFS is conditional on reached states [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
   - bai: structure vs action-conditioned categories within one programmatic channel [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16-17], while its visual and programmatic channel aggregates are close [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
   - The convergence is real at the level of "static structure is easier than interaction logic". It is *not* evidence that visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity. The evidence matrix should phrase it that way.
2. **Both benchmarks use an evaluated model family as judge, and neither tests self-preference.** chen uses Gemini-2.5-Pro, which is also evaluated (mid-table). bai uses Qwen3.7-Plus, which is also evaluated (lowest, after the B1 correction). Record this as a shared RQ4 weakness, not two separate ones.
3. **No repeated runs or CIs on headline scores in either benchmark**, and bai probably uses a single rollout (B5). This is a consistent limitation across the F2/F5 benchmark cluster and supports a gap claim about variance reporting, subject to the novelty-check rules.
4. **Difficulty gradient is consistent.** Algorithmic or game logic is hardest in chen (L4) and computation/interaction is weakest in bai. Neither paper controls for the size of each stratum: chen's L1 and L4 have about 9-12 tasks, and bai's category subsets differ (bai p. 17).
5. **Oracle construction from a running reference appears in two forms.** bai validates generated tests on the reference and adds human review [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8-9]. PropGen shows that LLM-derived behavioural properties are imprecise at a non-trivial rate (127/985 caused false positives) and need refinement plus human confirmation [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9]. Together they argue that auto-generated fidelity oracles need validation, which is relevant to the RQ5 study design.
6. **No duplicated or conflicting data across the three keys.** The other "Grok 4.6" mention in the project (kim2026programdistill) concerns a different benchmark, so it does not conflict. Once B1 is fixed, check that no downstream document (evidence matrix, gap report) has copied "Grok 4.6 lowest". As of this review, neither cites bai yet.

## Cross-cutting labelling note
In all three analyses, statements that something is absent ("no CIs", "not assessed", "confounded") are labelled [V] in the evidence tables. They are our appraisal of a missing item and should be [I], with the pages that were checked as the basis.

- Current: notes only that Gemini-2.5-Pro (thinking) has a lower VFS.
- Problem: all three thinking/non-thinking pairs have **lower VFS** with thinking (p. 8):
  - Claude-Sonnet-4: 60.20 vs 61.34
  - Claude-Opus-4: 58.67 vs 60.18
  - Gemini-2.5-Pro: 50.67 vs 53.18
- The authors' heading "Reasoning Enhancement Provides Consistent but Moderate Gains" (p. 9) is a conclusion beyond the data and should be [A].
- Correct text: "...thinking variants raise IFS and Final slightly in all three pairs but lower VFS in all three (60.20 vs 61.34; 58.67 vs 60.18; 50.67 vs 53.18) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). [A] Authors describe the gains as 'consistent but moderate' (p. 9). The Gemini Final difference is 0.05 points."

**C4 (moderate, §8 contains items that are not author-stated limitations).**
- Current: "[A] An LLM was used for grammar correction and language refinement of the paper (p. 21)". The alternative-weighting remark (p. 7) is also listed as self-critical.
- Problem: the LLM-use note is a disclosure (Appendix G), not a limitation. The weighting remark is a design rationale. The standard bars limitations in §8 that the authors never stated.
- Correct text: "Not reported: the paper has no limitations or threats-to-validity section. Design notes and disclosures (alternative weighting rejected, p. 7; agent-evaluation errors fixed, p. 9; LLM-assisted editing, p. 21) are recorded in Analyst notes." Move those items there.

**C5 (moderate, missing appraisal of the evaluator). §5; §9.**
- Problem: the paper calls the executor "deterministic ... built upon the browser-use library" (p. 6). Yet actions target elements by natural-language description (p. 17), and browser-use resolves descriptions with a model.
  - Which model resolves element descriptions, and whether replays are repeatable, is not reported.
  - "Deterministic" is an author claim [A].
  - It is also not reported whether the full benchmark was re-scored after the 3/100 evaluator failures were "rectified" (p. 9).
- Correct text, add to §5: "[A] Executor described as deterministic (p. 6); the model that resolves natural-language element descriptions (p. 17) and replay repeatability are not reported." Add to §9: "[I] Whether all 28 x 113 evaluations were re-run after the evaluator fixes (p. 9) is not reported."

**C6 (minor, missing "not reported"). §6 metric-weights bullet; §9 "Moderate human alignment".**
- Add: "Agreement among the five human raters is not reported; their judgements were aggregated (p. 17)." Likewise, nothing is reported about agreement among the three PhD students observing the agent (p. 9).

**C7 (hedging of the cross-paper claim). §12 last sentence; §13 strength note.**
- Current: "The same 'looks right, behaves wrong' pattern is reported across five platforms by [@bai2026recreationworld], which strengthens the finding."
- Problem: same as B8. bai's support is within-programmatic category gaps (p. 16-17 of bai). bai's visual channel is not higher than its programmatic channel in aggregate (bai p. 11).
- Correct text: "[I] Directionally consistent with [@bai2026recreationworld], which finds static structure reproduced better than action-conditioned behaviour within its programmatic tests; the two papers measure the gap differently, and here the gap is partly metric-induced (see §9)."

**C8 (labels). §13.**
- Rows "RQ4 | No repeated runs, confidence intervals or significance tests..." and "RQ5 | ...single-file output means code quality/maintainability is not assessed" are our appraisal of what is absent. The paper states neither. Label both **I**, with basis (p. 8-9; p. 7, 20).

**C9 (minor). §3 and §7 finding 3.**
- "28 models" counts three thinking variants separately, so there are 25 distinct base models (p. 8). Add as [I].
- "Proprietary models lead (Final 16.50-36.35)" overstates the separation: the best open-source model, Qwen3-VL (thinking) at 31.15, beats 11 of the 17 proprietary models (p. 8). Rephrase as "the top six are proprietary".

Checked and correct:
- 113 tasks / 100 sites; 200 -> 161 -> 113; 1,001 actions, 620 visual, 403 assertions; 35.4 s / 172.9 s; 19 resolutions; 10.62% mobile; L1-L4 and V1-V4 shares.
- Model group counts 17 / 9 / 2; GPT-5 36.35 / 24.39 / 64.25; the Final formula (0.7 x 24.39 + 0.3 x 64.25 = 36.35).
- 1 fps / 64 frames; HVS rubric 10 / 15 / 40 / 15 / 20; grid search, ρ = 0.57 / 0.65; 3 / 100 agent failures; case studies; Gemini-2.5-Pro as judge and evaluated model. All three quotes are verbatim.
- The derived per-category counts (§9) are correctly labelled [I].

---

## Cross-paper observations

1. **"Looks right, behaves wrong" is claimed as convergent evidence in both §12s, but the two papers measure different things** (see B8, C2, C7).
   - chen: VFS vs IFS, where VFS is conditional on reached states [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
   - bai: structure vs action-conditioned categories within one programmatic channel [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16-17], while its visual and programmatic channel aggregates are close [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
   - The convergence is real at the level of "static structure is easier than interaction logic". It is *not* evidence that visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity. The evidence matrix should phrase it that way.
2. **Both benchmarks use an evaluated model family as judge, and neither tests self-preference.** chen uses Gemini-2.5-Pro, which is also evaluated (mid-table). bai uses Qwen3.7-Plus, which is also evaluated (lowest, after the B1 correction). Record this as a shared RQ4 weakness, not two separate ones.
3. **No repeated runs or CIs on headline scores in either benchmark**, and bai probably uses a single rollout (B5). This is a consistent limitation across the F2/F5 benchmark cluster and supports a gap claim about variance reporting, subject to the novelty-check rules.
4. **Difficulty gradient is consistent.** Algorithmic or game logic is hardest in chen (L4) and computation/interaction is weakest in bai. Neither paper controls for the size of each stratum: chen's L1 and L4 have about 9-12 tasks, and bai's category subsets differ (bai p. 17).
5. **Oracle construction from a running reference appears in two forms.** bai validates generated tests on the reference and adds human review [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8-9]. PropGen shows that LLM-derived behavioural properties are imprecise at a non-trivial rate (127/985 caused false positives) and need refinement plus human confirmation [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9]. Together they argue that auto-generated fidelity oracles need validation, which is relevant to the RQ5 study design.
6. **No duplicated or conflicting data across the three keys.** The other "Grok 4.6" mention in the project (kim2026programdistill) concerns a different benchmark, so it does not conflict. Once B1 is fixed, check that no downstream document (evidence matrix, gap report) has copied "Grok 4.6 lowest". As of this review, neither cites bai yet.

## Cross-cutting labelling note
In all three analyses, statements that something is absent ("no CIs", "not assessed", "confounded") are labelled [V] in the evidence tables. They are our appraisal of a missing item and should be [I], with the pages that were checked as the basis.

## bai2026recreationworld — verdict: **needs-fixes** (10 fixes)

Ablira (72.73% Prog / 40.79% VLM, p. 46) was caught by the scrape detector, so the 0.10 aggregate cap applies (p. 38, p. 47); the table shows its pre-penalty channel scores [I]. Kartova escaped detection and kept 54.82% Prog / 14.63% VLM (34.72% average) (p. 47) — [V]."

Part of the IFS < VFS gap is therefore a property of the metrics, not only of the models." Add a matching sentence to §10 Construct.

  - Gemini-2.5-Pro: 50.67 vs 53.18
- The authors' heading "Reasoning Enhancement Provides Consistent but Moderate Gains" (p. 9) is a conclusion beyond the data and should be [A].
- Correct text: "...thinking variants raise IFS and Final slightly in all three pairs but lower VFS in all three (60.20 vs 61.34; 58.67 vs 60.18; 50.67 vs 53.18) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). [A] Authors describe the gains as 'consistent but moderate' (p. 9). The Gemini Final difference is 0.05 points."

**C4 (moderate, §8 contains items that are not author-stated limitations).**
- Current: "[A] An LLM was used for grammar correction and language refinement of the paper (p. 21)". The alternative-weighting remark (p. 7) is also listed as self-critical.
- Problem: the LLM-use note is a disclosure (Appendix G), not a limitation. The weighting remark is a design rationale. The standard bars limitations in §8 that the authors never stated.
- Correct text: "Not reported: the paper has no limitations or threats-to-validity section. Design notes and disclosures (alternative weighting rejected, p. 7; agent-evaluation errors fixed, p. 9; LLM-assisted editing, p. 21) are recorded in Analyst notes." Move those items there.

- Problem: the paper calls the executor "deterministic ... built upon the browser-use library" (p. 6). Yet actions target elements by natural-language description (p. 17), and browser-use resolves descriptions with a model.
  - Which model resolves element descriptions, and whether replays are repeatable, is not reported.
  - "Deterministic" is an author claim [A].
  - It is also not reported whether the full benchmark was re-scored after the 3/100 evaluator failures were "rectified" (p. 9).
- Correct text, add to §5: "[A] Executor described as deterministic (p. 6); the model that resolves natural-language element descriptions (p. 17) and replay repeatability are not reported." Add to §9: "[I] Whether all 28 x 113 evaluations were re-run after the evaluator fixes (p. 9) is not reported."

**C6 (minor, missing "not reported"). §6 metric-weights bullet; §9 "Moderate human alignment".**
- Add: "Agreement among the five human raters is not reported; their judgements were aggregated (p. 17)." Likewise, nothing is reported about agreement among the three PhD students observing the agent (p. 9).

**C7 (hedging of the cross-paper claim). §12 last sentence; §13 strength note.**
- Current: "The same 'looks right, behaves wrong' pattern is reported across five platforms by [@bai2026recreationworld], which strengthens the finding."
- Problem: same as B8. bai's support is within-programmatic category gaps (p. 16-17 of bai). bai's visual channel is not higher than its programmatic channel in aggregate (bai p. 11).
- Correct text: "[I] Directionally consistent with [@bai2026recreationworld], which finds static structure reproduced better than action-conditioned behaviour within its programmatic tests; the two papers measure the gap differently, and here the gap is partly metric-induced (see §9)."

**C8 (labels). §13.**
- Rows "RQ4 | No repeated runs, confidence intervals or significance tests..." and "RQ5 | ...single-file output means code quality/maintainability is not assessed" are our appraisal of what is absent. The paper states neither. Label both **I**, with basis (p. 8-9; p. 7, 20).

**C9 (minor). §3 and §7 finding 3.**
- "28 models" counts three thinking variants separately, so there are 25 distinct base models (p. 8). Add as [I].
- "Proprietary models lead (Final 16.50-36.35)" overstates the separation: the best open-source model, Qwen3-VL (thinking) at 31.15, beats 11 of the 17 proprietary models (p. 8). Rephrase as "the top six are proprietary".

Checked and correct:
- 113 tasks / 100 sites; 200 -> 161 -> 113; 1,001 actions, 620 visual, 403 assertions; 35.4 s / 172.9 s; 19 resolutions; 10.62% mobile; L1-L4 and V1-V4 shares.
- Model group counts 17 / 9 / 2; GPT-5 36.35 / 24.39 / 64.25; the Final formula (0.7 x 24.39 + 0.3 x 64.25 = 36.35).
- 1 fps / 64 frames; HVS rubric 10 / 15 / 40 / 15 / 20; grid search, ρ = 0.57 / 0.65; 3 / 100 agent failures; case studies; Gemini-2.5-Pro as judge and evaluated model. All three quotes are verbatim.
- The derived per-category counts (§9) are correctly labelled [I].

---

## Cross-paper observations

1. **"Looks right, behaves wrong" is claimed as convergent evidence in both §12s, but the two papers measure different things** (see B8, C2, C7).
   - chen: VFS vs IFS, where VFS is conditional on reached states [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
   - bai: structure vs action-conditioned categories within one programmatic channel [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16-17], while its visual and programmatic channel aggregates are close [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
   - The convergence is real at the level of "static structure is easier than interaction logic". It is *not* evidence that visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity. The evidence matrix should phrase it that way.
2. **Both benchmarks use an evaluated model family as judge, and neither tests self-preference.** chen uses Gemini-2.5-Pro, which is also evaluated (mid-table). bai uses Qwen3.7-Plus, which is also evaluated (lowest, after the B1 correction). Record this as a shared RQ4 weakness, not two separate ones.
3. **No repeated runs or CIs on headline scores in either benchmark**, and bai probably uses a single rollout (B5). This is a consistent limitation across the F2/F5 benchmark cluster and supports a gap claim about variance reporting, subject to the novelty-check rules.
4. **Difficulty gradient is consistent.** Algorithmic or game logic is hardest in chen (L4) and computation/interaction is weakest in bai. Neither paper controls for the size of each stratum: chen's L1 and L4 have about 9-12 tasks, and bai's category subsets differ (bai p. 17).
5. **Oracle construction from a running reference appears in two forms.** bai validates generated tests on the reference and adds human review [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8-9]. PropGen shows that LLM-derived behavioural properties are imprecise at a non-trivial rate (127/985 caused false positives) and need refinement plus human confirmation [@xiong2026propgen, p. 9]. Together they argue that auto-generated fidelity oracles need validation, which is relevant to the RQ5 study design.
6. **No duplicated or conflicting data across the three keys.** The other "Grok 4.6" mention in the project (kim2026programdistill) concerns a different benchmark, so it does not conflict. Once B1 is fixed, check that no downstream document (evidence matrix, gap report) has copied "Grok 4.6 lowest". As of this review, neither cites bai yet.

## Cross-cutting labelling note
In all three analyses, statements that something is absent ("no CIs", "not assessed", "confounded") are labelled [V] in the evidence tables. They are our appraisal of a missing item and should be [I], with the pages that were checked as the basis.

## Verdicts
| Key | Verdict | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| bai2026recreationworld | needs-fixes | 10 (B1-B10) |
| xiong2026propgen | pass-with-minor-fixes | 5 (X1-X5) |
| chen2025iwr | needs-fixes | 9 (C1-C9) |

## Most serious issues
1. **bai, wrong lowest-scoring model (B1).** Key finding 1 says "Grok 4.6 is lowest (9.15)". That column is actually **Qwen3.7-Plus**; Grok 4.6 is fourth at 36.73. The table headers are scrambled in the extracted text; the model order in Figure 1 (p. 1) and the scaffold settings in Table 8 (p. 28) settle it. This also changes the conflict-of-interest point: Qwen3.7-Plus is the visual judge and scores lowest, so no self-favouring is visible, though it was never tested.
2. **bai, findings generalised beyond their scope (B2).** The code-size, file-structure and final-check findings (89.4%, 92.3%, 83.8%, 23.6-47.5%, "highest/lowest LOC") cover only 4 of the 10 models, and the code-size comparison covers only desktop and Android. The analysis presents them as general.
3. **bai, scrape-penalty point resolved (B3).** The paper says the detector caught Ablira, yet its listed scores (72.73 / 40.79) are far above the 0.10 cap. So the case table shows scores before the penalty; that step is [I] but follows from the stated rule. Only Kartova (54.82 Prog), which escaped detection, shows a copied site keeping a real score. The RQ4 evidence row overstates the problem.
4. **chen, category tables misread (C1).** Tables 4-6 report the Final Score only (p. 16). "Functional fidelity falls" and "V4 hardest visually" describe the wrong metric. The pattern is also not monotonic: L2 and L3 are about equal, several models score L3 above L2, and V3 beats V2.
5. **chen, headline gap partly built into the metrics (C2).** The visual score is averaged only over checkpoints the page actually reached (p. 7), while the functional score counts all actions. So "functionality lags visual fidelity for every model" is partly a property of how the scores are defined, and the analysis never says so.
6. **xiong, author overlap understated (X1).** Ting Su co-authored Genie, Odin, PBFDroid and Kea. So three of the four comparison tools in the bug-finding comparison come from the authors' own group, and the scope check "validated by consulting the tool authors" is not independent. Also, PropGen uses the app's manifest and a string list from static analysis (pp. 4-5), so it is not purely black-box for our reverse-engineering framing (X2).

## Your flagged points
- **chen per-category counts:** the arithmetic is right (about 9 L1 and 12 L4 tasks) and correctly labelled [I].
- **bai 13.64% → 44 tasks:** correctly labelled [I], but 3 of 22 fits too. The paper does say runs failing isolation checks are invalidated (p. 9) and uses "evaluator-valid" subsets (p. 11, p. 20); the analysis should cite that.
- **bai single rollout:** related to "not reported" rollouts, the paper gives indirect evidence. The one-rollout interface comparison's scores (35.05 / 31.00) equal the main Table 11 entries, so the main benchmark is probably one rollout per task (B5, [I]).
- **xiong kappas:** 0.91 / 0.82 / 0.81 match p. 7; the two-column layout did not garble them.
- **83.8%:** this figure is in bai, not xiong, and it is correct (pp. 15-16).

## Other fixes and cross-paper points
- **Labels:** across all three evidence tables, statements that something is missing ("no CIs", "not assessed", "confounded") are labelled [V]; they are our appraisal and should be [I] (B7, C8, X5).
- **Convergence claim:** both §12 sections cite each other's "looks right, behaves wrong" result as agreement. In bai the overall visual and functional scores are about equal (57.92 vs 58.19 for the top model); its support comes from category gaps inside the functional tests. This needs hedging (B8, C7).
- **chen thinking variants (C3):** all three thinking variants have *lower* visual scores, not just Gemini.
- **chen limitations (C4):** §8 lists the LLM-editing disclosure as a limitation; the paper states no limitations.
- **bai transfer experiment (B6):** there is no control arm, and gains are measured against the first evaluated checkpoint, not the starting model.
- **Shared weaknesses:** both benchmarks use a model they also evaluate as judge and have no repeated runs.
- **No conflicting data:** the three papers do not contradict each other. Once B1 is fixed, check that "Grok 4.6 lowest" has not been copied into any downstream document; the evidence matrix and gap report do not cite bai yet.
